Full-Spectrum Graph Neural Network: Expressive and Scalable

Xiaohan Wang Affiliation: Division of Mathematical Sciences, School of Physical and Mathematical Sciences, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore 637371, Singapore    Deyu Bo Affiliation: Division of Mathematical Sciences, School of Physical and Mathematical Sciences, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore 637371, Singapore    Longlong Li Affiliation: Division of Mathematical Sciences, School of Physical and Mathematical Sciences, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore 637371, Singapore    Kelin Xia Affiliation: Division of Mathematical Sciences, School of Physical and Mathematical Sciences, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore 637371, Singapore Correspondence to: xiakelin@ntu.edu.sg
Abstract

It is well established that spectral graph neural networks (GNNs) can universally approximate node signals; however, their expressive power remains bounded by the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler–Lehman test, which is mirrored in their lack of universality for higher-order signals. To go beyond this bound, we propose the Full-Spectrum GNN (FSpecGNN), a second-order generalization of classical spectral GNNs. FSpecGNN advances spectral filtering in two perspectives: (1) it lifts the signal from the node domain to the node-pair domain; and (2) it extends the univariate spectral filter over eigenvalues to a bivariate filter over eigenvalue pairs. We show that classical spectral GNNs arise as a diagonal special case of FSpecGNN, and prove that FSpecGNN can be at most as expressive as Local 2-GNN while universally approximating node-pair signals, the latter being particularly beneficial for heterophilic graph learning. Moreover, FSpecGNN admits scalable implementations that avoid explicit node-pair-level computations; combined with a low-rank approximation that reduces full-spectrum convolution to a combination of polynomial spectral filters, it enables learning on large graphs. Empirically, FSpecGNN validates the predicted expressivity and delivers strong performance on heterophilic benchmarks.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) is a standard paradigm for learning from data with underlying graph structure, combining feature transformations with graph propagations. A central line of research studies the expressivity of GNNs, which provides a principled lens for comparing the representational power of different architectures in learning from graph-structured data. A mainstream framework for such analyses characterizes expressivity by a model’s ability to distinguish non-isomorphic graphs, ranging from the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler–Lehman (1-WL) test (Xu et al., 2019) to more recent homomorphism-based expressivity (Zhang et al., 2024), yielding a well-established expressiveness hierarchy for GNNs. Within this hierarchy, a standard way to surpass 1-WL is to lift message passing from the node domain to higher-order domains, such as node pairs V×VV\times V and, more generally, kk-tuples (Morris et al., 2019; Morris et al., 2020). In contrast, spectral GNNs, which parameterize propagation as Laplacian filtering, have a comparatively incomplete expressivity picture: while they are universal for node-signal approximation (Wang and Zhang, 2022; Roth and Liebig, 2025), their ability to distinguish non-isomorphic graphs remains bounded by 1-WL (Wang and Zhang, 2022). This raises a natural question: what is the spectral counterpart of lifting that enables spectral GNNs to systematically go beyond 1-WL?

Our contributions. We propose the full-spectrum GNN (FSpecGNN) as a second-order generalization of spectral GNNs; the same construction also extends directly to higher orders. Concretely, instead of filtering node signals x∈ℝVx\in\mathbb{R}^{V}, full-spectrum filtering operates on node-pair signals ε∈ℝV×V\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times V} and generalizes classical spectral filtering

U⁡(gλ⊙(U⊤​x))=∑ig⁡(λi)​ui​ui⊤​x\displaystyle U\big(g_{\lambda}\odot(U^{\top}x)\big)=\sum_{i}g(\lambda_{i})\,u_{i}u_{i}^{\top}x (1)
⇓\displaystyle\Downarrow
U⁡(Gλ⊙(U⊤​ε​U))​U⊤=∑i,jg⁡(λi,λj)​ui​ui⊤​ε​uj​uj⊤\displaystyle U\big(G_{\lambda}\odot(U^{\top}\varepsilon U)\big)U^{\top}=\sum_{i,j}g(\lambda_{i},\lambda_{j})\,u_{i}u_{i}^{\top}\varepsilon\,u_{j}u_{j}^{\top} (2)

where L=U​Λ​U⊤L=U\Lambda U^{\top} is the eigendecomposition of the graph Laplacian with eigenvectors U=[u1,…,un]U=[u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}] and eigenvalues Λ=diag⁡(λ1,…,λn)\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}). FSpecGNN naturally extends the classic univariate spectral filter gλ=(g⁡(λi))1≤i≤|V|g_{\lambda}=(g(\lambda_{i}))_{1\leq i\leq|V|} to a bivariate matrix Gλ=(g⁡(λi,λj))1≤i,j≤|V|G_{\lambda}=(g(\lambda_{i},\lambda_{j}))_{1\leq i,j\leq|V|}. Proposition 3.3 further shows that Eq. (1) is recovered within Eq. (2) via a diagonal embedding.

FSpecGNN is expressive: it can surpass the 1-WL upper bound. In particular, under sufficient conditions, Theorem 3.8 shows that FSpecGNN matches the distinguishing power of Local 2-GNN (Zhang et al., 2024). Complementarily, Theorem 3.4 establishes a universal approximation result for 11-dimensional node-pair signals. FSpecGNN is also scalable: Section 3.4 discusses implementations of FSpecGNN to avoid explicit computations in the node-pair domain. We further propose a low-rank approximation in Eq. (3), which approximates a full-spectrum convolution using only a small number of polynomial spectral filters (e.g., BernConv (He et al., 2021)). This leads to implementations Eq. (5) whose computational complexity is comparable to that of existing spectral GNNs.

We further demonstrate the utility of FSpecGNN on heterophilic graph learning tasks, where adjacent nodes often carry different labels and thus naive neighborhood aggregation can be detrimental (Luan et al., 2023). To understand heterophily from a spectral perspective, we study the optimal convolution that maximally separates representations across different labels. Theorem 4.1 shows that the resulting convolution suppresses (and, in particular, assigns zero weight to) positions corresponding to inter-class connections. We then prove a fundamental limitation: Theorem 4.2 establishes that such an optimal convolution cannot be realized within the class of classical spectral convolutions. In contrast, FSpecGNN can realize this optimal operator via a slight modification of our implementation. Together, these results identify heterophily as an inherently second-order phenomenon and highlight the importance of scalable second-order architectures such as FSpecGNN.

Finally, we evaluate FSpecGNN on substructure-counting benchmarks (Zhang et al., 2024), where the empirical results align with our expressivity predictions. Moreover, FSpecGNN is substantially more efficient in practice, achieving roughly 5×5\times lower runtime than the corresponding spatial second-order baselines and the lowest peak GPU memory among all compared methods. We also assess FSpecGNN on standard heterophilic node-classification benchmarks and demonstrate consistent gains over a range of representative baselines.

Full-spectrum convolution admits a simple view as propagation on the Cartesian product graph G​□​GG\square G over node set V×VV\times V, where (u,v)(u,v) is adjacent to (u′,v′)(u^{\prime},v^{\prime}) iff u=u′u=u^{\prime} and (v,v′)∈E(v,v^{\prime})\in E, or v=v′v=v^{\prime} and (u,u′)∈E(u,u^{\prime})\in E. Concretely, L⊗InL\otimes I_{n} (resp. In⊗LI_{n}\otimes L) propagates along the second (resp. first) coordinate while keeping the other fixed. As a special case, if we enforce simultaneous propagation along both coordinates by restricting the bivariate function to g⁡(s,t)=h⁡(s+t)g(s,t)=h(s+t) for some univariate hh, the induced operator reduces to g⁡(L⊕L)g(L\oplus L), where L⊕L:=L⊗In+In⊗LL\oplus L\;:=\;L\otimes I_{n}+I_{n}\otimes L, is the Kronecker sum of Laplacians. Moreover, L⊕LL\oplus L is exactly the Laplacian of the Cartesian product graph G​□​GG\square G (Brouwer and Haemers, 2011), so g⁡(L⊕L)g(L\oplus L) implements simultaneous propagation on both coordinates. In this sense, g⁡(L⊕L)g(L\oplus L) is a degraded second-order convolution: the signal is lifted to node pairs, but the filter is constrained to be univariate.

3.2 Classical Spectral Filtering as a Subfamily

Classical spectral filters can be characterized as a subfamily of full-spectrum filters via diagonal embedding.

Proposition 3.3.

Given node signal x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, define the diagonal embedding ℰ⁡(x):=∑i=1nx^i​ui​ui⊤\mathcal{E}(x)\;:=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{x}_{i}\,u_{i}u_{i}^{\top} with x^i:=ui⊤​x\hat{x}_{i}:=u_{i}^{\top}x, and the projection 𝒫⁡(H):=∑i=1n(ui⊤​H​ui)​ui\mathcal{P}(H)\;:=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}(u_{i}^{\top}Hu_{i})\,u_{i} for H∈ℝn×nH\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. Then

𝒫⁡(g⁡(L⊗In,In⊗L)​ℰ​(x))=U​g~​(Λ)​U⊤​x,\mathcal{P}\!\left(g(L\otimes I_{n},\ I_{n}\otimes L)\,\mathcal{E}(x)\right)\;=\;U\,\tilde{g}(\Lambda)\,U^{\top}x,

where g~​(Λ)≔diag​(g⁡(λi,λi))1≤i≤n\tilde{g}(\Lambda)\coloneqq\mathrm{diag}(g(\lambda_{i},\lambda_{i}))_{1\leq i\leq n}, recovering the classical spectral filtering.

The proof is provided in Appendix C (Proposition C.3). From this perspective, classical spectral filters can be viewed as diagonal-spectrum filters, obtained by restricting the full-spectrum filter to the diagonal of the paired spectrum.

3.3 Full-Spectrum GNN and Its Expressivity

Based on the full-spectrum filtering, we propose the full spectrum GNN, i.e., FSpecGNN. Given node features X∈ℝn×d1X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{1}} and node-pair features E∈ℝn×n×d2E\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n\times d_{2}}, we first lift them to representations in node-pair domain via Hu​v=ϕ⁡(Xu,Xv,Eu​v)∈ℝd,H_{uv}=\phi(X_{u},X_{v},E_{uv})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, where ϕ\phi can be either a hand-crafted encoder or a neural network. Stacking all pairwise representations yields a tensor H∈ℝn×n×dH\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n\times d}, which we reshape into a matrix H∈ℝn2×dH\in\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}\times d}. A full-spectrum convolution layer is then defined as

H′=σ⁡(g⁡(L⊗In,In⊗L)​H​W),H^{\prime}\;=\;\sigma\!\bigl(g(L\otimes I_{n},\,I_{n}\otimes L)\,H\,W\bigr),

where gg is a learnable bivariate function. Depending on the choice of readout, the filtered representations H′H^{\prime} can be used to produce edge/node/graph-level predictions.

Now We consider two complementary notions of expressivity for spectral GNNs. The first is specific to spectral methods and concerns their ability to universally approximate graph signals. The second is a model’s ability to distinguish non-isomorphic graphs.

Parallel to Wang and Zhang (2022), who showed the linear spectral GNN can universally approximate one-dimensional signals on VV, we prove that the linear FSpecGNN can universally approximate one-dimensional signals on V×VV\times V, with proof provided in Appendix D (Theorem D.1).

Theorem 3.4.

Linear FSpecGNN, obtained by removing the nonlinear activation, can produce any one-dimensional node-pair signal prediction if the normalized Laplacian L~\tilde{L} has no multiple eigenvalues and the input representation HH contain all paired frequency components, namely, (U⊗U)⊤​H(U\otimes U)^{\top}H is non-zero for every index (u,v)∈V×V(u,v)\in V\times V.

We next study the ability of FSpecGNN to distinguish non-isomorphic graphs. Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a finite graph with an initial node labeling ℓ(0):V→Σ\ell^{(0)}:V\to\Sigma, where Σ\Sigma is a countable label set. We adopt the standard definitions of 1-WL and Local 2-GNN from Zhang et al. (2024).

Definition 3.5.

The 1-dimensional Weisfeiler–Lehman test refines node labels by

ℓ(t)​(v)=HASH⁡(ℓ(t−1)​(v),{{ℓ(t−1)​(u):u∈N⁡(v)}}),\ell^{(t)}(v)=\mathrm{HASH}\Bigl(\ell^{(t-1)}(v),\{\!\!\{\ell^{(t-1)}(u):u\in N(v)\}\!\!\}\Bigr),

where N⁡(v)N(v) denotes the neighborhood of vv and HASH\mathrm{HASH} is an perfect hash function. The process iterates until stabilization. Two graphs are distinguished by 1-WL if the multisets of node labels differ at some iteration.

Definition 3.6.

The local 2-GNN operates on ordered node pairs (u,v)∈V×V(u,v)\in V\times V. It initializes ℓ(0)​(u,v)=(ℓ(0)​(u),ℓ(0)​(v),𝐚𝐭𝐩⁡(u,v))\ell^{(0)}(u,v)=\big(\ell^{(0)}(u),\ell^{(0)}(v),\mathbf{atp}(u,v)\big), where the atomic type is 𝐚𝐭𝐩⁡(u,v)=(𝟏u=v,𝟏(u,v)∈E)\mathbf{atp}(u,v)=(\mathbf{1}_{u=v},\mathbf{1}_{(u,v)\in E}). For t≥0t\geq 0, define multisets ℳu←v(t):={{ℓ(t)​(w,v):w∈N⁡(u)}}\mathcal{M}^{(t)}_{u\leftarrow v}:=\{\!\!\{\ell^{(t)}(w,v):w\in N(u)\}\!\!\} and ℳv←u(t):={{ℓ(t)​(u,w):w∈N⁡(v)}}\mathcal{M}^{(t)}_{v\leftarrow u}:=\{\!\!\{\ell^{(t)}(u,w):w\in N(v)\}\!\!\}, and update

ℓ(t+1)​(u,v)=HASH⁡(ℓ(t)​(u,v),ℳu←v(t),ℳv←u(t)).\ell^{(t+1)}(u,v)=\mathrm{HASH}\bigl(\ell^{(t)}(u,v),\mathcal{M}^{(t)}_{u\leftarrow v},\mathcal{M}^{(t)}_{v\leftarrow u}\bigr).

The process iterates until stabilization.

First, consider FSpecGNN that realizes g⁡(L⊗In,In⊗L)g(L\otimes I_{n},\,I_{n}\otimes L) via bivariate polynomial pp. By stacking the pairwise label ℓ(0)​(u,v)\ell^{(0)}(u,v) into a matrix ℒ∈ℝn2×d\mathcal{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}\times d} for some dd, We show that the resulting model has expressivity upper-bounded by Local 22-GNN.

Theorem 3.7.

Let pp be any polynomial of total degree at most KK, and define the filtered linear representation ℒ′=p⁡(L⊗I,I⊗L)​ℒ​W\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=p(L\otimes I,I\otimes L)\mathcal{L}W. Let χ(u,v)(k)\chi^{(k)}_{(u,v)} denote the color of index (u,v)(u,v) after kk iterations of the Local 22-GNN refinement. Then for any (u1,v1),(u2,v2)∈V×V(u_{1},v_{1}),(u_{2},v_{2})\in V\times V and any matrix WW,

χ(u1,v1)(K)=χ(u2,v2)(K)⟹ℒ′​(u1,v1)=ℒ′​(u2,v2).\chi^{(K)}_{(u_{1},v_{1})}=\chi^{(K)}_{(u_{2},v_{2})}\Longrightarrow\mathcal{L}^{\prime}(u_{1},v_{1})=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}(u_{2},v_{2}).

In contrast, by allowing bivariate polynomials, there exists a polynomial q⁡(s,t)q(s,t) such that the FSpecGNN induced by qq achieves greater expressivity than local 2-GNNs.

Theorem 3.8.

Let χ(u,v)(∞)\chi^{(\infty)}_{(u,v)} denote the stable Local 22-GNN color on index (u,v)(u,v). If LL has a simple spectrum and U⊤​ℒ​UU^{\top}\mathcal{L}U is index-wise nonzero, then there exists a bivariate polynomial qq and a matrix WW, such that the filtered representation ℒ′=q⁡(L⊗In,In⊗L)​ℒ​W\mathcal{L}^{\prime}=q(L\otimes I_{n},\ I_{n}\otimes L)\mathcal{L}W satisfies

ℒ′​(u1,v1)=ℒ′​(u2,v2)⟹χ(u1,v1)(∞)=χ(u2,v2)(∞).\mathcal{L}^{\prime}(u_{1},v_{1})=\mathcal{L}^{\prime}(u_{2},v_{2})\Longrightarrow\chi^{(\infty)}_{(u_{1},v_{1})}=\chi^{(\infty)}_{(u_{2},v_{2})}.

Proofs are provided in Appendix D (Theorem D.3, D.6). Note that Theorem 3.8 is an existence result: in practice, the learned filter may or may not realize the specific polynomial qq guaranteed by the theorem. Consequently, the empirical expressivity of FSpecGNN can vary across tasks and may be slightly weaker or stronger than that of Local 22-GNNs, depending on the parameterization and optimization.

3.4 Scalability of FSpecGNN

A main challenge for second-order methods is scalability. Concretely, filtering in the node-pair domain is intractable, as it requires multiplying an n2×n2n^{2}\times n^{2} matrix by an n2n^{2}-dimensional vector. In this section, we discuss implementations of FSpecGNN, especially those that avoid these costs, including explicit eigendecomposition and node-pair–level computations. These implementations mainly involve choosing parameterizations of the bivariate function gg.

Route I: direct learning of g⁡(λi,λj)g(\lambda_{i},\lambda_{j}). When the graph is small, we can explicitly compute the eigendecomposition and learn the bivariate filter gθ:ℝ2→ℝg_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} directly, e.g., using an MLP. In computing a full-spectrum convolution g⁡(L⊗In,In⊗L)​Hg(L\otimes I_{n},\,I_{n}\otimes L)H, we follow Definition 3.1, constructing GλG_{\lambda} by (Gλ)i​j=gθ​(λi,λj),(G_{\lambda})_{ij}\;=\;g_{\theta}(\lambda_{i},\lambda_{j}), and apply Gλ⊙((U⊗U⊤)​ε)G_{\lambda}\odot\big((U\otimes U^{\top})\varepsilon\big) followed by inverse GFT transform, where ε\varepsilon is one channel of HH and we apply the same convolution to all channels. This route is impractical for large graphs, as eigendecomposition requires O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) and GFT requires O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) time.

Route II: polynomial parameterization of g⁡(λi,λj)g(\lambda_{i},\lambda_{j}). We parameterize the filter by a polynomial q⁡(L⊗In,In⊗L)=∑p=0K∑q=0Kαp​q​(Lp⊗Lq).q(L\otimes I_{n},I_{n}\otimes L)=\sum_{p=0}^{K}\sum_{q=0}^{K}\alpha_{pq}(L^{p}\otimes L^{q}). Learning gg is then reduced to learning the coefficient matrix (αp​q)(\alpha_{pq}). A key computational benefit is that we never explicitly construct Lp⊗Lq∈ℝn2×n2L^{p}\otimes L^{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}\times n^{2}}, instead, we exploit by Lemma 2.3 to have (Lp⊗Lq)​vec​(ε)=vec⁡(Lq​ε​Lp),(L^{p}\otimes L^{q})\mathrm{vec}(\varepsilon)=\mathrm{vec}(L^{q}\varepsilon L^{p}), reducing computations to n×nn\times n matrix multiplications. Although we avoid computations in the node-pair domain, we still have (K+1)2(K+1)^{2} polynomial terms; even with a recursive implementation, applying the filter still costs O⁡(K2)O(K^{2}) left/right multiplications, which becomes expensive for high-degree polynomial filters.

Further scalability via tensor decomposition. To mitigate the at least quadratic dependence on KK, we exploit the tensor-product structure of bivariate polynomial filters. Proofs are provided in Appendix C (Proposition C.4).

Proposition 3.9.

Let P⁡(s,t)=∑i+j≤Kai​j​si​tjP(s,t)=\sum_{i+j\leq K}a_{ij}\,s^{i}t^{j} be a bivariate polynomial, and denote by A=(ai​j)A=(a_{ij}) its coefficient matrix. Then the induced operator P⁡(L⊗In,In⊗L)P(L\otimes I_{n},\;I_{n}\otimes L) admits a decomposition of the form

P⁡(L⊗In,In⊗L)=∑r=1Rfr​(L)⊗hr​(L)P(L\otimes I_{n},\;I_{n}\otimes L)=\sum_{r=1}^{R}f_{r}(L)\otimes h_{r}(L)

for univariate polynomials {fr,hr}\{f_{r},h_{r}\} satisfying deg⁡(fr)≤K\mathrm{deg}(f_{r})\leq K and deg⁡(hr)≤K\mathrm{deg}(h_{r})\leq K for all rr, if and only if R≥rank⁡(A)R\geq\mathrm{rank}(A).

In particular, a low-rank approximation of the coefficient matrix AA yields a truncated tensor decomposition with only a small number of terms:

𝒯LS≔∑r=1Sfr​(L)⊗hr​(L),S≪rank⁡(A).\mathcal{T}_{L}^{S}\;\coloneqq\;\sum_{r=1}^{S}f_{r}(L)\otimes h_{r}(L),\qquad S\ll\mathrm{rank}(A). (3)

Thus we only need to perform O⁡(S​K)O(SK) matrix multiplications with degree-KK univariate polynomials frf_{r} and hrh_{r}.

4 Application to Heterophilic Graph Learning

4.1 Necessity of Off-diagonal Components

Classical spectral GNN restricts to diagonal spectral convolutions g⁡(L)=∑ig⁡(λi)​ui​ui⊤.g(L)=\sum_{i}g(\lambda_{i})\,u_{i}u_{i}^{\top}. Equivalently, for any such convolution matrix C=g⁡(L)C=g(L), U⊤​C​UU^{\top}CU is diagonal. In contrast, spatial message passing GNNs typically learn convolution operators whose spectral expansions over the basis {ui​uj⊤}\{u_{i}u_{j}^{\top}\} contain non-zero off-diagonal components, i.e., U⊤​C​UU^{\top}CU generally non-diagonal. We answer the following question in this section: are such off-diagonal components merely incidental artifacts of spatial message passing, or do they play a principled and necessary role in learning?

We study this question in heterophilic graph learning, where adjacent nodes often carry different labels and classical models such as GCNs can degrade substantially. To understand heterophily from a spectral perspective, we firstly characterize an optimal convolution operator that maximally separates representations across different labels, equivalently, maximally contracts representations within the same label, under suitable idealized assumptions.

Model Assumption. Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a graph with |V|=n|V|=n, whose nodes are partitioned into kk classes Π={V1,…,Vk}\Pi=\{V_{1},\dots,V_{k}\} with |Va|=na|V_{a}|=n_{a} and ∑a=1kna=n\sum_{a=1}^{k}n_{a}=n. For each class a∈{1,…,k}a\in\{1,\dots,k\}, we randomly draw a class mean vector ma∈ℝdm_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} independently from the unit sphere 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1}.

Conditioned on these class means, node features are generated independently across nodes according to their class labels. Specifically, for each node i∈Vaii\in V_{a_{i}}, the feature vector xi∼𝒟ai,x_{i}\sim\mathcal{D}_{a_{i}}, where each class-conditional distribution 𝒟a\mathcal{D}_{a} on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} has mean mam_{a} and covariance matrix Σa⪰0\Sigma_{a}\succeq 0. We denote by X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} the resulting feature matrix, whose ii-th row is xi⊤x_{i}^{\top}. For convenience, we write τa:=tr⁡(Σa)\tau_{a}:=\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_{a}) for the total feature variance of class aa, and assume τa>0\tau_{a}>0 for all aa.

Under this model, we now specify a measurement to quantify class separability after graph propagation. Rather than adopting a Bayesian formulation (Luan et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024), we consider a deterministic classwise mean squared error

ℒ⁡(C):=∑a=1k1na​∑p∈Va𝔼​‖Yp−ma‖22,\mathcal{L}(C):=\sum_{a=1}^{k}\frac{1}{n_{a}}\sum_{p\in V_{a}}\mathbb{E}\,\bigl\|Y_{p}-m_{a}\bigr\|_{2}^{2}, (4)

where Y:=C​X∈ℝn×dY:=CX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} denotes the propagated feature matrix, YpY_{p} is its pp-th row, and mam_{a} is the class-wise mean.

Eq. (4) is well suited to our setting: ℒ⁡(C)\mathcal{L}(C) is differentiable with respect to CC, and the optimal solution C∗:=arg⁡minC⁡ℒ⁡(C)C^{\ast}:=\arg\min_{C}\mathcal{L}(C) admits a closed-form characterization.

Theorem 4.1.

Let C∗C^{*} be a minimizer of ℒ⁡(C)\mathcal{L}(C). Assume τa​na≥τ0>0\tau_{a}n_{a}\geq\tau_{0}>0 for each class a∈{1,…,k}a\in\{1,\dots,k\}, where τ0\tau_{0} is a fixed positive constant lower bound. Then, as the feature dimension d→∞d\to\infty, C∗C^{*} becomes asymptotically block-diagonal with respect to the class partition Π\Pi, with

(C∗)Va×Vb→ℙ{sa∗​JVa,a=b,0,a≠b,sa∗→ℙ1na+τa.(C^{*})_{V_{a}\times V_{b}}\;\xrightarrow{\ \mathbb{P}\ }\;\begin{cases}s_{a}^{*}\,J_{V_{a}},&a=b,\\[4.0pt] 0,&a\neq b,\end{cases}\qquad s_{a}^{*}\xrightarrow{\ \mathbb{P}\ }\dfrac{1}{n_{a}+\tau_{a}}.

The proof is provided in Appendix E (Theorem E.9). It shows that the inter-class blocks of optimal convolution C⋆C^{\star} vanish asymptotically, while intra-class blocks converge to class-dependent constants. We now prove that such convolutions cannot be realized by classical spectral filters.

Theorem 4.2.

Given a connected graph GG, there exists a GG-dependent integer K≥1K\geq 1 such that for any K<k≤nK<k\leq n, there exists a kk-partition V=V1∪⋯∪VkV=V_{1}\cup\cdots\cup V_{k} with label assignment yi=a⇔vi∈Vay_{i}=a\iff v_{i}\in V_{a} such that the following holds: if a diagonal-spectral operator C=g⁡(L)C=g(L) satisfies

Ci​j=0whenever ​yi≠yj,C_{ij}=0\quad\text{whenever }y_{i}\neq y_{j},

then necessarily C=α​InC=\alpha I_{n} for some α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}.

See Theorem E.12 for the proof. It shows that any spectral filter of the form C=g⁡(L)C=g(L) that enforces Cu​v=0C_{uv}=0 whenever ℓ⁡(u)≠ℓ⁡(v)\ell(u)\neq\ell(v) must degenerate to C=α​IC=\alpha I, and thus cannot approximate the optimal convolution in Theorem 4.1. Therefore, achieving the optimal class-separability convolution in general requires off-diagonal components, highlighting their importance for heterophilic graph learning.

The argument is supported by analysis of optimal convolutions across datasets with varying degrees of heterophily. Let Wi​j:=(U⊤​C​U)i​j2.W_{ij}:=(U^{\top}\!CU)_{ij}^{2}. denote the spectral energy associated with the eigengraph component ui​uj⊤u_{i}u_{j}^{\top}. For a bandwidth parameter δ∈[0,2]\delta\in[0,2], we define the near-diagonal energy ratio EC​(δ):=∑|λi−λj|≤δWi​j/∑i,jWi​j.E_{C}(\delta):=\sum_{|\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}|\leq\delta}W_{ij}/\sum_{i,j}W_{ij}. Empirically, EC∗​(δ)E_{C^{*}}(\delta) of optimal convolution C∗C^{*} exhibits a clear trend: as the level of heterophily increases, spectral energy shifts away from the diagonal, see Figure 3, indicating a growing reliance on off-diagonal components.

4.2 How FSpecGNN Models Off-diagonal

We provide a scalable implementation of FSpecGNN that models off-diagonal components without explicitly constructing node pair-domain operators.

We exploit the low-rank approximation 𝒯LS\mathcal{T}_{L}^{S} in Eq. (3), and take a small rank SS, e.g., S=1S=1. Let 𝒯L1=f⁡(L)⊗h⁡(L)\mathcal{T}_{L}^{1}=f(L)\otimes h(L), where ff and hh are univariate polynomial spectral filters. Given an initial convolution ε∈ℝn×n\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, we have OPENf⁡(L)⊗h⁡(L))​ε=h⁡(L)​ε​f​(L)f(L)\otimes h(L))\varepsilon=h(L)\,\varepsilon\,f(L) by Lemma 2.3. Thus a full-spectrum convolution layer can be implemented as

H′=σ⁡(h⁡(L)​ε​f​(L)​H​W),H^{\prime}=\sigma\big(h(L)\,\varepsilon\,f(L)\,H\,W), (5)

where H∈ℝn×dH\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} is a matrix of node representations. In practice, we can set both ff and hh to be classical filters such as ChebConv (Defferrard et al., 2016), ChebIIConv (He et al., 2022) or BernConv (He et al., 2021). The initial convolution can be either fixed or learnable, and we choose ε=I+α​GAT\varepsilon\;=\;I+\alpha\mathrm{GAT}, where GAT is a single-layer GAT (Velickovic et al., 2018) and α\alpha is a learnable scalar.

Let L=U​Λ​U⊤L=U\Lambda U^{\top}. Expanding the linear convolution in Eq. (5) in the eigengraph basis gives

h⁡(L)​ε​f​(L)=∑i,jh⁡(λi)​f​(λj)​(ui⊤​ε​uj)​ui​uj⊤.h(L)\,\varepsilon\,f(L)=\sum_{i,j}h(\lambda_{i})\,f(\lambda_{j})\,\bigl(u_{i}^{\top}\varepsilon u_{j}\bigr)\,u_{i}u_{j}^{\top}.

Therefore, an off-diagonal ui​uj⊤u_{i}u_{j}^{\top} (i≠ji\neq j) appears whenever the coefficient ui⊤​ε​uju_{i}^{\top}\varepsilon u_{j} is nonzero, see Corollary C.7 for more explanations. GAT-based initialization fits this case, since the resulting ε\varepsilon is feature-dependent and generally does not commute with the Laplacian LL. In this view, GAT induces feature-dependent off-diagonal mixing, while 𝒯LS\mathcal{T}_{L}^{S} spectrally reweights both diagonal and off-diagonal components, tuning their balance via the frequency-pair response.

Complexity. Let KfK_{f} and KhK_{h} denote the polynomial degrees of ff and hh. The linear convolution in Eq. (5) can be computed as H1=f⁡(L)​HH_{1}=f(L)H, H2=ε​H1H_{2}=\varepsilon H_{1}, and H′=h⁡(L)​H2H^{\prime}=h(L)H_{2}. Using sparse multiplications, the two polynomial spectral filters incur a cost of O⁡((Kf+Kh)​m​d)O((K_{f}+K_{h})md), while the single-layer GAT propagation costs O⁡(m​d)O(md) up to head-dependent constants. Consequently, the overall complexity is O⁡(K​m​d)O(Kmd) with K≈Kf+KhK\approx K_{f}+K_{h}, matching the order of classical polynomial spectral layers such as BernConv. For a general rank SS in Eq. (3), the cost increases linearly in SS.

5 Experiments

We benchmark FSpecGNN on three representative tasks: node classification on heterophilic datasets, homomorphism counting, and cycle counting. For the counting tasks, our primary goal is not to push state-of-the-art performance; rather, we use them as controlled evaluations to validate the theoretical predictions derived in our analysis.

Datasets. For heterophilic node classification, we conduct experiments on eight widely used benchmark datasets, including four small heterophilic graphs (Texas, Wisconsin, Chameleon, and Squirrel) and four large-scale heterophilic graphs (Roman Empire, Minesweeper, Tolokers, and Questions). Following Platonov et al. (2023), we use the directed clean versions of Chameleon and Squirrel, removing duplicate nodes. For all datasets, we adopt the sparse split strategy of Liu and Wang (2025), randomly partitioning nodes into training/validation/test sets with ratios of 2.5%/2.5%/95%2.5\%/2.5\%/95\%.

For homomorphism counting, we adopt the benchmark of Zhao et al. (2022) and evaluate graph-level homomorphism counts as well as node/edge-anchored homomorphism count regression, using the same template graphs as Zhang et al. (2024). For (chordal) cycle counting, following Huang et al. (2023), we evaluate graph-level and node/edge-anchored (chordal) cycle subgraph count regression, again selecting the same subgraphs as Zhang et al. (2024).

Baselines. For heterophilic node classification, our baselines include five representative spectral GNNs: ChebNet, GPRGNN (Chien et al., 2021), BernNet, JacobiConv (Wang and Zhang, 2022), and ChebNetII, with results reported in Liu and Wang (2025). For homomorphism and cycle counting, we compare against MPNN, Subgraph GNN, Local 2-GNN, and Local 2-FGNN, adopting the results reported by Zhang et al. (2024), as well as Spectral Invariant GNN with results from Gai et al. (2025).

5.1 Heterophilic Node Classification

We adopt FSpecGNN in form of Eq. (5) with detailed implementation described in Section 4.2, yielding three variants denoted by FSpecGNN(Cheb/ChebII/Bern), respectively. The results are reported in the last three rows of Table 1. ROC-AUC is reported on Minesweeper, Tolokers, and Questions, while test accuracy is reported on the remaining datasets. Across all datasets, each variant consistently improves upon its corresponding base filter (e.g., FSpecGNN(Cheb) vs. ChebNet, and similarly for ChebII and Bern). Moreover, for every dataset, the best-performing FSpecGNN variant surpasses all preceding spectral baselines in Table 1.

5.2 GNN Expressivity

We adopt Route I in Section 3.4 and parameterize the spectral response gg using a two-layer MLP. Since a single spectral layer can aggregate global information, we do not follow the five propagation layers used in Zhang et al. (2024); instead, we use fewer layers with a larger hidden dimension, resulting in a comparable model size (approximately 300300K parameters) to the baselines. Apart from the above modifications, we keep all remaining hyperparameters and setups identical to Zhang et al. (2024).

The reported performance is measured by normalized mean absolute error (MAE). Results are summarized in Tables 2 and 3. In Table 2, cell colors indicate MAE ranges: blue for <0.025<0.025, green for [0.025,0.05)[0.025,0.05), orange for [0.05,0.1)[0.05,0.1), and red for ≥0.1\geq 0.1. Overall, the empirical results align with our theoretical predictions. In particular, Theorems 3.7 and 3.8 suggest that FSpecGNNs should have expressivity comparable to Local 2-GNNs when equipped with sufficiently expressive spectral filters. This argument is supported by experiments: on all benchmarks, FSpecGNN achieves performance comparable to Local 2-GNN, and even outperforms it on some datasets. Moreover, compared to Spectral Invariant GNN, which also leverages graph spectral information, FSpecGNN achieves substantially lower MAE on these benchmarks.

5.3 Ablation Study

Table 4 studies the contribution of architectural components in FSpecGNN(Cheb) on heterophilic node classification. The full model uses two spectral filters: the in-filter hh, applied to the input features before eigenspace interaction, and the out-filter ff, applied after interaction to refine the propagated representation. Removing off-diagonal interactions consistently degrades performance across datasets, underscoring the necessity of modeling cross-eigenspace coupling. Ablating both the in-filter hh and the off-diagonal interaction reduces the model to ChebNet, yielding performance consistent with the baseline.

5.4 Time and Space Overhead

We evaluate the computational efficiency of models on the homomorphism- and cycle-counting benchmarks in Table 5. For each model, we report the average time per iteration, aggregated over graph/node/edge levels across both homomorphism- and cycle-counting tasks, and the peak GPU memory usage, taken as the maximum over all tasks. Task-wise results are provided in Appendix F. Notably, MPNN is realized on the lifted node-pair domain representation and reduces to MPNN only through a degenerate message passing, so it retains second-order computational overhead. Table 5 shows that FSpecGNN achieves substantially lower runtime and the lowest peak GPU memory among all compared second-order spatial GNNs. This advantage is mainly due to the fact that spectral filters can achieve long-range propagation with much fewer layers and the moderate graph sizes in these benchmarks.

6 Related Works

Several recent GNN architectures are closely related, yet they differ from our work in perspectives of the signal domain, the spectral filter, and the analysis focus. Specformer (Bo et al., 2023) learns a set-to-set map on the graph spectrum, but the resulting operator remains diagonal in the eigenbasis; our framework instead parameterizes g⁡(λi,λj)g(\lambda_{i},\lambda_{j}) to enable off-diagonal spectral interactions. CITRUS (Einizade et al., 2024) leverages Cartesian product graphs and continuous diffusion for scalable learning on multi-domain data; our focus instead stays within a single graph and its internal spectral interactions. STSGNN (Chen et al., 2025) designs second-order spectral filters for spatio-temporal modeling by using two Laplacians from the spatial and temporal domains; in contrast, we study second-order spectral filters based on a single graph and analyze their expressivity and scalability. Finally, Spectral Invariant GNNs (Gai et al., 2025) inject spectral invariants into GNNs and study homomorphism expressivity, using spectral information in a positional-encoding-like manner rather than parameterizing a spectral filter. More related works are discussed in Appendix A.

7 Conclusion

We propose FSpecGNN as a second-order generalization of spectral GNNs. It can surpass the expressivity limits of 11-WL, while admitting scalable implementations that extend to large graphs. Overall, as a second-order spectral GNN, FSpecGNN is both expressive and scalable, making it well suited to tasks with inherently second-order structure.

Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning, specifically in spectral graph neural networks. Our contributions are methodological and are intended for general-purpose use. We do not anticipate substantial ethical concerns or negative societal consequences beyond those commonly associated with machine learning research.

Appendix A More Related Work

A.1 Spectral GNN Architectures

Spectral GNNs implement graph convolution as a Laplacian filter g⁡(L)g(L), but exact eigendecomposition is typically avoided via scalable approximations. Defferrard et al. (2016) introduced truncated Chebyshev polynomial parameterizations to realize localized spectral filtering, and GCN (Kipf and Welling, 2017) can be viewed as a first-order simplification that yields an efficient, widely used propagation rule. Subsequent work increasingly emphasizes stable and flexible spectral-response parameterizations beyond vanilla Chebyshev expansions: ChebNetII (He et al., 2022) attributes ChebNet’s weaker performance to poorly behaved learned coefficients, while BernNet (He et al., 2021) learns arbitrary spectral filters via Bernstein approximation, enabling controlled realization of diverse frequency responses. In parallel, diffusion-based formulations connect propagation to PageRank: PPNP/APPNP (Gasteiger et al., 2019) derive personalized-PageRank propagation decoupled from prediction, and GPR-GNN (Chien et al., 2021) generalizes this view by learning generalized PageRank weights to adapt across homophily/heterophily regimes. Finally, recent research finds that the choice of polynomial basis materially affects optimization and practical performance, motivating a sequence of methods that select or learn improved polynomial bases for spectral filtering (Wang and Zhang, 2022; Guo and Wei, 2023). Moreover, spectral methods have been explored for heterophily by moving beyond purely low-pass smoothing: either by injecting learnable high-pass responses or by combining multiple spectral filters to adapt across homophily/heterophily regimes (Bo et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2023). Recent studies also highlight the role of polynomial bases under heterophily, motivating heterophily-aware and universal basis construction beyond predefined Laplacian bases (Huang et al., 2024).

A.2 Expressivity of Spectral GNNs

Expressivity has been a central theme in the GNN literature, and is most commonly studied through the WL-based hierarchy. Xu et al. (2019) shows that standard neighborhood aggregation is at most as powerful as 11-WL for graph discrimination, which catalyzed extensive WL-based analyses and the development of higher-order GNNs matching stronger WL variants (Morris et al., 2019; Maron et al., 2019; Morris et al., 2020). Going beyond this coarse WL lens, (Zhang et al., 2024) propose homomorphism expressivity as a finer quantitative hierarchy for comparing substructure-counting capabilities. In contrast, theoretical understanding of spectral GNN expressivity is relatively limited: Wang and Zhang (2022) establish universality results for spectral filtering on node signals, while also relating spectral models to 11-WL limitations. More recently, (Roth and Liebig, 2025) extend the universality analysis to multi-channel (MIMO) settings. Gai et al. (2025) study spectral-invariant architectures that inject spectral information as basis-invariant positional encodings; their expressivity has been characterized via WL- and homomorphism-based analysis.

Appendix B Discussions and Potential Limitations

B.1 Discussions on FSpecGNN

Extending Full-Spectrum Filtering to Higher Orders. Although we instantiate the framework at second order, i.e. the node-pair domain, the same construction extends canonically to kk-th order signals on VkV^{k}. Let LL be a chosen graph Laplacian on GG and let InI_{n} be the n×nn\times n identity. On the kk-fold product domain, define the commuting operators

L(1):=L⊗In⊗(k−1),L(2):=In⊗L⊗In⊗(k−2),…,L(k):=In⊗(k−1)⊗L.L^{(1)}:=L\otimes I_{n}^{\otimes(k-1)},\quad L^{(2)}:=I_{n}\otimes L\otimes I_{n}^{\otimes(k-2)},\ \ldots,\ L^{(k)}:=I_{n}^{\otimes(k-1)}\otimes L.

A kk-variate spectral filter can then be parameterized as g⁡(L(1),…,L(k))g\!\left(L^{(1)},\ldots,L^{(k)}\right). For example, the third-order case acts on V3V^{3} via

g⁡(L⊗In⊗In,In⊗L⊗In,In⊗In⊗L),g(L\otimes I_{n}\otimes I_{n},\ I_{n}\otimes L\otimes I_{n},\ I_{n}\otimes I_{n}\otimes L),

which propagates along each coordinate while keeping the others fixed. This higher-order viewpoint provides a systematic route to designing spectral GNNs that operate on kk-tuple domains, and enables a systematic connection between higher-order spectral constructions and the expressiveness hierarchy of GNNs, e.g. (Zhang et al., 2024).

Beyond Graph Laplacians. A further direction is to move beyond graph Laplacians to Laplacians defined on higher-dimensional combinatorial structures, such as simplicial or cell complexes. These domains admit Laplacian operators, e.g. Hodge Laplacians, acting on pp-cochains, including edge/face-signals, whose spectra encode topology/geometry-related modes that are invisible to purely node-level models. From this perspective, our use of the Cartesian product provides one concrete instance of how additional structure induces a corresponding notion of propagation: full-spectrum filtering can be interpreted as propagation along different coordinates of a product graph. For richer higher-order structures, the induced propagation is generally governed not by the graph Laplacian alone, but by the Laplacians intrinsic to the underlying domain, suggesting that analogous spectral formalisms could be developed to capture these more complex propagation patterns. For example, cell complex neural networks generalize message passing via boundary/coboundary operators, inducing propagation patterns determined by higher-order incidence relations (Hajij et al., 2020), and BScNets further exploit block Hodge-Laplacians to couple interactions across different dimensions, enabling information mixing between cells of different orders (Chen et al., 2022). Developing spectral analyses and learning methods for these Laplacians remains under-explored and is a natural extension of our perspective.

B.2 Potential Limitations and Future Work

Universal Approximation on Multi-channel Node-pair Signals Our discussion on universal approximation focuses on 11-dimensional node-pair signals. In practice, approximation capacity can be strengthened by adopting a MIMO design similar to Roth and Liebig (2025), i.e., learning multiple input/output channels with channel mixing, which is standard in spectral GNNs and can be incorporated into our framework directly.

Underexplored implementation choices for FSpecGNN.

While our framework is general, our empirical instantiation explores only a limited portion of the design space. First, for heterophily node classification we adopt a particular initial convolution in the form of the pair-domain signal, ε=I+α​GAT\varepsilon=I+\alpha\,\mathrm{GAT}, which is a reasonable but by no means canonical choice; alternative initial convolutions may yield better performance. Second, for scalability we mainly use the low-rank parameterization with S=1S=1, i.e., a single filter pair (f,h)(f,h). The general form allows S>1S>1 with multiple filter pairs, raising additional questions on how to compose and coordinate these components effectively. A systematic exploration of ε\varepsilon and multi-component designs is left to future work.

Appendix C Algebraic Properties and Parameterizations of Full-Spectrum Filters

C.1 Basic Properties

Definition C.1.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be an undirected graph. The Cartesian product graph G​□​GG\square G is the graph with vertex set V×VV\times V, where two vertices (u,v)(u,v) and (u′,v′)(u^{\prime},v^{\prime}) are adjacent if and only if either u=u′u=u^{\prime} and (v,v′)∈E(v,v^{\prime})\in E, or v=v′v=v^{\prime} and (u,u′)∈E(u,u^{\prime})\in E.

Under the above convention, the action of L⊗InL\otimes I_{n} and In⊗LI_{n}\otimes L can be described explicitly as follows: for (u,v)∈V×V(u,v)\in V\times V,

((L⊗In)​ε)​(u,v)=(ε​L)​(u,v)\displaystyle\bigl((L\otimes I_{n})\varepsilon\bigr)(u,v)=(\varepsilon L)(u,v) =∑v′∈Vε⁡(u,v′)​Lv′,v,\displaystyle=\sum_{v^{\prime}\in V}\varepsilon(u,v^{\prime})\,L_{v^{\prime},v},
((In⊗L)​ε)​(u,v)=(L​ε)​(u,v)\displaystyle\bigl((I_{n}\otimes L)\varepsilon\bigr)(u,v)=(L\varepsilon)(u,v) =∑u′∈VLu,u′​ε​(u′,v).\displaystyle=\sum_{u^{\prime}\in V}L_{u,u^{\prime}}\,\varepsilon(u^{\prime},v).

That is, right (resp. left) multiplication by LL propagates the signal by changing the second (resp. first) coordinate of G​□​GG\square G while keeping the other fixed, see the first row of Figure 1 for an illustration.

(L⊗In)a=La⊗In,(In⊗L)b=In⊗Lb,(L\otimes I_{n})^{a}=L^{a}\otimes I_{n},\qquad(I_{n}\otimes L)^{b}=I_{n}\otimes L^{b},

We restate and prove Proposition 3.3 as follows.

Proposition C.3.

Define the diagonal embedding ℰ:ℝn→ℝn×n\mathcal{E}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} and the projection 𝒫:ℝn×n→ℝn\mathcal{P}:\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} by

ℰ⁡(x):=∑i=1nx^i​ui​ui⊤,x^i:=ui⊤​x,\mathcal{E}(x)\;:=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{x}_{i}\,u_{i}u_{i}^{\top},\qquad\hat{x}_{i}:=u_{i}^{\top}x,

𝒫⁡(H):=∑i=1n(ui⊤​H​ui)​ui.\mathcal{P}(H)\;:=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}(u_{i}^{\top}Hu_{i})\,u_{i}.

Then

𝒫⁡(g⁡(L⊗In,In⊗L)​ℰ​(x))=U​diag​(g⁡(λ1,λ1),…,g⁡(λn,λn))​U⊤​x.\mathcal{P}\!\left(g(L\otimes I_{n},\ I_{n}\otimes L)\,\mathcal{E}(x)\right)\;=\;U\,\mathrm{diag}\!\big(g(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{1}),\dots,g(\lambda_{n},\lambda_{n})\big)\,U^{\top}x.

Equivalently, if we define a univariate spectral response g~​(λ):=g​(λ,λ)\tilde{g}(\lambda):=g(\lambda,\lambda), then

𝒫⁡(g⁡(L⊗In,In⊗L)​ℰ​(x))=U​g~​(Λ)​U⊤​x,\mathcal{P}\!\left(g(L\otimes I_{n},\ I_{n}\otimes L)\,\mathcal{E}(x)\right)\;=\;U\,\tilde{g}(\Lambda)\,U^{\top}x,

which recovers the classical spectral filtering with response g~\tilde{g}.

Proof.

We first record two elementary facts: (i) By definition, ℰ⁡(x)∈span​{ui​ui⊤}i=1n\mathcal{E}(x)\in\mathrm{span}\{u_{i}u_{i}^{\top}\}_{i=1}^{n}; (ii) L⁡(ui​ui⊤)=(L​ui)​ui⊤=λi​ui​ui⊤,L(u_{i}u_{i}^{\top})=(Lu_{i})u_{i}^{\top}=\lambda_{i}\,u_{i}u_{i}^{\top}, and (ui​ui⊤)​L=ui​(ui⊤​L)=λi​ui​ui⊤(u_{i}u_{i}^{\top})L=u_{i}(u_{i}^{\top}L)=\lambda_{i}\,u_{i}u_{i}^{\top} as L​ui=λi​uiLu_{i}=\lambda_{i}u_{i} and LL is symmetric. Therefore we have

g⁡(L⊗In,In⊗L)​(ui​ui⊤)=g⁡(λi,λi)​ui​ui⊤.g(L\otimes I_{n},\ I_{n}\otimes L)\,(u_{i}u_{i}^{\top})\;=\;g(\lambda_{i},\lambda_{i})\,u_{i}u_{i}^{\top}.

g⁡(L⊗In,In⊗L)​ℰ​(x)=∑i=1ng⁡(λi,λi)​x^i​ui​ui⊤.g(L\otimes I_{n},\ I_{n}\otimes L)\,\mathcal{E}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}g(\lambda_{i},\lambda_{i})\,\hat{x}_{i}\,u_{i}u_{i}^{\top}.

Using orthonormality uk⊤​ui=δk​iu_{k}^{\top}u_{i}=\delta_{ki},

uk⊤​(ui​ui⊤)​uk=(uk⊤​ui)​(ui⊤​uk)=δk​i,u_{k}^{\top}(u_{i}u_{i}^{\top})u_{k}=(u_{k}^{\top}u_{i})(u_{i}^{\top}u_{k})=\delta_{ki},

hence the coefficient of uku_{k} is exactly g⁡(λk,λk)​x^kg(\lambda_{k},\lambda_{k})\hat{x}_{k}. Thus

𝒫⁡(g⁡(L⊗In,In⊗L)​ℰ​(x))=∑k=1ng⁡(λk,λk)​x^k​uk=U​diag​(g⁡(λ1,λ1),…,g⁡(λn,λn))​U⊤​x,\mathcal{P}\!\left(g(L\otimes I_{n},\ I_{n}\otimes L)\,\mathcal{E}(x)\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}g(\lambda_{k},\lambda_{k})\,\hat{x}_{k}\,u_{k}=U\,\mathrm{diag}(g(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{1}),\dots,g(\lambda_{n},\lambda_{n}))\,U^{\top}x,

C.2 Tensor Decomposition of Full-Spectrum Filters.

Note that (L⊗I)i​(I⊗L)j=(I⊗L)j​(L⊗I)i=Li⊗Lj(L\otimes I)^{i}(I\otimes L)^{j}=(I\otimes L)^{j}(L\otimes I)^{i}=L^{i}\otimes L^{j}. We restate and prove Proposition 3.9 as follows.

Proposition C.4.

Let P⁡(I⊗L,L⊗I)P(I\otimes L,\,L\otimes I) be a bivariate polynomial of total degree nn in the two matrix variables I⊗LI\otimes L and L⊗IL\otimes I. We write

P⁡(I⊗L,L⊗I)=∑0≤i,j≤ni+j≤nci​j​(I⊗L)i​(L⊗I)j=∑0≤i,j≤ni+j≤nci​j​Li⊗Lj,P(I\otimes L,\,L\otimes I)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq i,j\leq n\\ i+j\leq n\end{subarray}}c_{ij}\,(I\otimes L)^{i}(L\otimes I)^{j}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq i,j\leq n\\ i+j\leq n\end{subarray}}c_{ij}\,L^{\,i}\otimes L^{\,j},

where the coefficients are collected into a (n+1)×(n+1)(n{+}1)\times(n{+}1) matrix A=(ci​j)0≤i,j≤nA=(c_{ij})_{0\leq i,j\leq n}. Here, ci​j=0c_{ij}=0 whenever i+j>ni+j>n. Then there exist polynomial pairs {(fr,hr)}r=1R\{(f_{r},h_{r})\}_{r=1}^{R} with deg⁡fr≤n\deg f_{r}\leq n and deg⁡hr≤n\deg h_{r}\leq n for all rr, such that

P⁡(I⊗L,L⊗I)=∑r=1Rfr​(L)⊗hr​(L),P(I\otimes L,\,L\otimes I)\;=\;\sum_{r=1}^{R}f_{r}(L)\otimes h_{r}(L),

if and only if R≥rank⁡(A)R\geq\mathrm{rank}(A).

Lemma C.5.

Let A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be a square matrix. Then

  1. 1.

    If rank⁡(A)=R\mathrm{rank}(A)=R, there exist vectors α1,…,αR∈ℝn\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and β1,…,βR∈ℝn\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that

    A=∑i=1Rαi​βi⊤.A\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{R}\alpha_{i}\beta_{i}^{\top}.
  2. 2.

    Conversely, if AA can be written as

    A=∑i=1Rαi​βi⊤,A=\sum_{i=1}^{R}\alpha_{i}\beta_{i}^{\top},

    then rank⁡(A)≤R\mathrm{rank}(A)\leq R.

In particular, the minimal number of rank-one matrices {αi​βi⊤}\{\alpha_{i}\beta_{i}^{\top}\} required in such a decomposition equals rank⁡(A)\mathrm{rank}(A).

Proof.

(1) Since rank⁡(A)=R\mathrm{rank}(A)=R, the column space of AA has dimension RR. Choose a basis c1,…,cR∈ℝnc_{1},\dots,c_{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} for the column space and set C=[c1⋯cR]∈ℝn×RC=[\,c_{1}\ \cdots\ c_{R}\,]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times R}. Then there exists D∈ℝR×nD\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times n} such that A=C​DA=CD. Writing DD row-wise as D=[b1⋯bR]⊤D=[\,b_{1}\ \cdots\ b_{R}\,]^{\top} with bi∈ℝnb_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we obtain

A=∑i=1Rci​bi⊤,A=\sum_{i=1}^{R}c_{i}b_{i}^{\top},

where we set αi=ci\alpha_{i}=c_{i}, βi=bi\beta_{i}=b_{i}.

(2) Suppose A=∑i=1Rαi​βi⊤A=\sum_{i=1}^{R}\alpha_{i}\beta_{i}^{\top}. For any x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

A​x=∑i=1Kαi​(βi⊤​x)∈span⁡{α1,…,αK}.Ax=\sum_{i=1}^{K}\alpha_{i}(\beta_{i}^{\top}x)\in\mathrm{span}\{\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{K}\}.

Hence the column space of AA is contained in span​{αi}\mathrm{span}\{\alpha_{i}\}, which has dimension at most KK. Therefore rank⁡(A)≤K\mathrm{rank}(A)\leq K. Combining with part (1), the minimal number of rank-one matrices required is exactly rank⁡(A)\mathrm{rank}(A). ∎

Proof of Proposition C.4.

We may write

D.1 Universal Approximation on Node-Pair Signals

At the node level, we have the following result reformulated from (Wang and Zhang, 2022), which states that any spectral GNN expressed as a polynomial of the normalized Laplacian is upper-bounded in expressive power by 11-WL\mathrm{WL}.

Z=H(K)∘H(K−1)∘⋯∘H(0)(XW).Z=H^{(K)}\circ H^{(K-1)}\circ\cdots\circ H^{(0)}(XW).

Recall that the 1-WL color refinement is defined by

χ1−WL,(k+1)​(i)=𝗁𝖺𝗌𝗁⁡(χ1−WL,(k)​(i),{{χ1−WL,(k)​(j):j∈N⁡(i)}}),\chi^{\mathrm{1-WL},(k+1)}(i)=\mathsf{hash}\!\left(\chi^{\mathrm{1-WL},(k)}(i),\;\big\{\!\!\big\{\chi^{\mathrm{1-WL},(k)}(j):j\in N(i)\big\}\!\!\big\}\right),

Consequently, if two nodes have the same 1-WL color after the kk-th iteration, then they receive identical updates under H(k)H^{(k)}, i.e.,

χG1−WL,(k)​(i)=χG1−WL,(k)​(j)⟹hi(k)=hj(k).\chi^{\mathrm{1-WL},(k)}_{G}(i)=\chi^{\mathrm{1-WL},(k)}_{G}(j)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad h_{i}^{(k)}=h_{j}^{(k)}.

By induction over kk, all intermediate representations remain equal, and therefore the final outputs coincide:

χG1−WL,(K+1)​(i)=χG1−WL,(K+1)​(j)⟹y⁡(i)=y⁡(j).\chi^{\mathrm{1-WL},(K+1)}_{G}(i)=\chi^{\mathrm{1-WL},(K+1)}_{G}(j)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y(i)=y(j).

∎

A subtle conceptual issue arises when bridging the apparent inconsistency noted in (Wang and Zhang, 2022). In (Wang and Zhang, 2022), Proposition 4.3 shows that, for a fixed graph and fixed node features, a linear GNN with a degree-KK spectral polynomial filter is bounded by (K+1)(K\!+\!1) iterations of the 1-WL test, as formulated above. On the other hand, Theorem 4.1 establishes that, under the “no multiple eigenvalues” and “no missing frequency components” conditions, linear spectral GNNs enjoy a universal approximation property and can, in principle, map all nodes to distinct outputs. This seems at odds with the well-known fact that 1-WL often fails to distinguish certain pairs of vertices.

To bridge this gap, (Wang and Zhang, 2022) argues that their spectral conditions imply that 1-WL can distinguish all “non-isomorphic nodes” (Corollary 4.4), and moreover that the graph admits no nontrivial labeled automorphisms (Theorem 4.6). Consequently, every pair of nodes becomes non-isomorphic in their sense, and 1-WL must distinguish all vertices, thereby removing the apparent contradiction with Proposition 4.3.

Although the formal statements of Theorem 4.5 and Theorem 4.6 are mathematically correct, the way they are invoked to resolve the apparent inconsistency is not justified, as it is important to distinguish between two similar yet inequivalent notions of node equivalence. One notion is automorphism-based equivalence: two vertices are considered “isomorphic” if they lie in the same orbit of the labeled automorphism group Aut⁡(G,ℓ)\mathrm{Aut}(G,\ell). The other is 11-WL\mathrm{WL} equivalence: two vertices receive the same stable 11-WL\mathrm{WL} color or, equivalently, have isomorphic unrolling trees (Morris et al., 2020). In general, these notions do not coincide. Even with a trivial automorphism group, 1-WL may still collapse all nodes to a single color. A classical example is the Frucht graph: it is 33-regular and asymmetric, i.e. its automorphism group consists only of the identity, yet 11-WL\mathrm{WL} with uniform initial labels fails to distinguish any of its vertices.

The reconciliation between universality and the 11-WL\mathrm{WL} upper bound does not actually stem from the absence of nontrivial automorphisms. Rather, it is the universality assumptions themselves that severely constrain the admissible graph-signal pairs: a simple Laplacian spectrum, together with labels having full spectral support, enforces a highly non-degenerate labeling. When 11-WL\mathrm{WL} is run on such labels, its refinement becomes much more discriminative; in fact, combined with the upper bound in Proposition 4.3, universality forces the stable 11-WL\mathrm{WL} partition on (G,ℓ)(G,\ell) to refine all the way down to singletons, since any two vertices mapped to different values by a universal linear spectral GNN must already be separated by 11-WL\mathrm{WL}.

We restate and prove Theorem 3.7 as follows.

Theorem D.3.

Definition D.4.

Let G=(V,E,ℓ)G=(V,E,\ell) be a labeled graph. For a pair (u,v)∈V×V(u,v)\in V\times V, define its depth-kk local unrolling tree, denoted by

L​-​UNRG(k)​(u,v),\mathrm{L\text{-}UNR}_{G}^{(k)}(u,v),

recursively as follows.

  • •

    For k=0k=0, L​-​UNRG(0)​(u,v)\mathrm{L\text{-}UNR}_{G}^{(0)}(u,v) consists of a single root, whose vertex label is the initial pair label

    ε(u,v)=(ℓ(u),ℓ(v),𝕀[u=v],𝕀[{u,v}∈E]).\varepsilon(u,v)=\bigl(\ell(u),\ell(v),\mathbb{I}[u=v],\mathbb{I}[\{u,v\}\in E]\bigr).
  • •

    1. 1.

      for every u′∈NG​(u)u^{\prime}\in N_{G}(u), one child whose attached subtree is L​-​UNRG(k−1)​(u′,v)\mathrm{L\text{-}UNR}_{G}^{(k-1)}(u^{\prime},v), with the edge from the root to this child labeled by 11;

Two such trees are said to be isomorphic if there exists a bijection between their vertex sets that preserves: (i) the root, (ii) the parent–child relation, (iii) the vertex labels, and (iv) the directed edge labels in {1,2}\{1,2\}.

Lemma D.5 (Morris et al. (2020)).

For any labeled graph GG, any (u1,v1),(u2,v2)∈V×V(u_{1},v_{1}),(u_{2},v_{2})\in V\times V, and any k≥0k\geq 0,

if and only if

L​-​UNRG(k)​(u1,v1)≅L​-​UNRG(k)​(u2,v2).\mathrm{L\text{-}UNR}_{G}^{(k)}(u_{1},v_{1})\cong\mathrm{L\text{-}UNR}_{G}^{(k)}(u_{2},v_{2}).

Appendix E An Analysis of Spectral Filters for Class-Wise Separability

E.1 Optimal Convolution under Classwise Separability

E.1.1 Setting and Notation

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a graph with |V|=n|V|=n. Nodes are partitioned into kk classes Π={V1,…,Vk}\Pi=\{V_{1},\dots,V_{k}\} with |Va|=na|V_{a}|=n_{a} and ∑ana=n\sum_{a}n_{a}=n. For each class a∈{1,…,k}a\in\{1,\dots,k\}, we associate a mean vector ma∈ℝdm_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, drawn independently and uniformly at random from the unit sphere 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1}. Conditioned on these means, node features are drawn independently according to their class labels:

xi∼𝒟ai,ai​ such that ​i∈Vai,x_{i}\ \sim\ \mathcal{D}_{a_{i}},\qquad a_{i}\text{ such that }i\in V_{a_{i}},

where each class distribution 𝒟a\mathcal{D}_{a} on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} has mean mam_{a} and finite covariance Σa⪰0\Sigma_{a}\succeq 0. Denote by X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} the resulting feature matrix with rows xi⊤x_{i}^{\top}, and write τa:=tr⁡(Σa)\tau_{a}:=\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_{a}) for the total variance of class aa, where we assume τa>0\tau_{a}>0 for every aa. This model can be viewed as a high-dimensional isotropic mixture in which class means are randomly oriented and features fluctuate around them with bounded covariance.

A (linear) convolution is a matrix C∈ℝn×nC\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} producing Y:=C​XY:=CX. We evaluate CC by the classwise mean-regression MSE

ℒ⁡(C):=∑a=1k1na​∑p∈Va𝔼​‖Yp−ma‖22.\mathcal{L}(C)\ :=\ \sum_{a=1}^{k}\frac{1}{n_{a}}\sum_{p\in V_{a}}\ \mathbb{E}\,\big\|\,Y_{p}-m_{a}\big\|_{2}^{2}. (9)
Definition E.1.

Let Π={V1,…,Vk}\Pi=\{V_{1},\dots,V_{k}\} be the class partition of the node set VV with |Va|=na|V_{a}|=n_{a}. For each class aa, let 𝔖na\mathfrak{S}_{n_{a}} be the permutation group acting on the indices VaV_{a}, and define the product group

𝒢:=∏a=1k𝔖na,\mathcal{G}\ :=\ \prod_{a=1}^{k}\mathfrak{S}_{n_{a}},

whose elements π=(π1,…,πk)\pi=(\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{k}) act on VV by independently permuting the nodes within each class. The corresponding permutation matrix PπP_{\pi} acts on vectors or matrices as a block permutation operator.

A matrix C∈ℝn×nC\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is said to be classwise permutation equivariant if

C=Pπ​C​Pπ⊤,∀π∈𝒢.C\ =\ P_{\pi}\,C\,P_{\pi}^{\top},\qquad\forall\,\pi\in\mathcal{G}.

Equivalently, CC commutes with the representation of 𝒢\mathcal{G} on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

For any matrix CC, its Reynolds average with respect to 𝒢\mathcal{G} is defined as

C¯:=𝔼π∼Unif⁡(𝒢)​[Pπ​C​Pπ⊤],\overline{C}\ :=\ \mathbb{E}_{\pi\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{G})}\big[P_{\pi}\,C\,P_{\pi}^{\top}\big],

which is classwise permutation equivariant and thus belongs to the commutant of 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

E.1.2 Algebraic Structure and a Bias–Variance Decomposition

Before analyzing the loss ℒ⁡(C)\mathcal{L}(C) in its explicit form, we first show that the Reynolds average of any matrix CC can only decrease the loss. This allows us to restrict attention, without loss of generality, to classwise-equivariant matrices.

Lemma E.2.

Let 𝒢=∏a=1k𝔖na\mathcal{G}=\prod_{a=1}^{k}\mathfrak{S}_{n_{a}} act on indices by classwise permutations, and define the Reynolds average of C∈ℝn×nC\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} by C¯\overline{C}. Then the classwise mean-regression loss satisfies

ℒ⁡(C¯)≤ℒ⁡(C).\mathcal{L}(\overline{C})\ \leq\ \mathcal{L}(C).
Proof.

For fixed feature matrix X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, with ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{F} denoting the Frobenius norm, write

ℓ⁡(C,X):=∑a=1k1na​‖(C​X)a−𝟏na​ma⊤‖F2.\ell(C;X)\ :=\ \sum_{a=1}^{k}\frac{1}{n_{a}}\big\|\,(CX)_{a}-\mathbf{1}_{n_{a}}m_{a}^{\top}\,\big\|_{F}^{2}.

The map C↦C​XC\mapsto CX is linear, and A↦∑a1na​‖Aa−𝟏​ma⊤‖F2A\mapsto\sum_{a}\frac{1}{n_{a}}\|A_{a}-\mathbf{1}m_{a}^{\top}\|_{F}^{2} is a quadratic form in AA, and thus convex. Hence ℓ⁡(C,X)\ell(C;X) is convex in CC, and taking expectation over XX preserves convexity, so ℒ⁡(C)=𝔼X​[ℓ⁡(C,X)]\mathcal{L}(C)=\mathbb{E}_{X}[\ell(C;X)] is convex in CC. Since C¯\overline{C} is the group average of linear transforms of CC, convexity gives

ℓ⁡(C¯,X)=ℓ⁡(𝔼π​[Pπ​C​Pπ⊤],X)≤𝔼π​ℓ​(Pπ​C​Pπ⊤,X).\ell(\overline{C};X)\ =\ \ell\!\big(\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[P_{\pi}CP_{\pi}^{\top}];X\big)\ \leq\ \mathbb{E}_{\pi}\,\ell(P_{\pi}CP_{\pi}^{\top};X).

Taking expectation in XX and exchanging the order of expectations,

ℒ⁡(C¯)=𝔼X​ℓ​(C¯,X)≤𝔼π​𝔼X​ℓ​(Pπ​C​Pπ⊤,X).\mathcal{L}(\overline{C})\ =\ \mathbb{E}_{X}\ell(\overline{C};X)\ \leq\ \mathbb{E}_{\pi}\,\mathbb{E}_{X}\ell(P_{\pi}CP_{\pi}^{\top};X).

For any π∈𝒢\pi\in\mathcal{G},

ℓ⁡(Pπ​C​Pπ⊤,X)=ℓ⁡(C,Pπ⊤​X),\ell(P_{\pi}CP_{\pi}^{\top};X)=\ell(C;P_{\pi}^{\top}X),

because (Pπ​C​Pπ⊤)​X=Pπ​[C⁡(Pπ⊤​X)](P_{\pi}CP_{\pi}^{\top})X=P_{\pi}[C(P_{\pi}^{\top}X)] and Frobenius norms are invariant under left multiplication by the permutation matrices PπaP_{\pi_{a}} within each class. Under the classwise i.i.d. model in Section E.1.1, Pπ⊤​XP_{\pi}^{\top}X and XX are identically distributed, so 𝔼X​ℓ​(C,Pπ⊤​X)=𝔼X​ℓ​(C,X)=ℒ⁡(C)\mathbb{E}_{X}\ell(C;P_{\pi}^{\top}X)=\mathbb{E}_{X}\ell(C;X)=\mathcal{L}(C). Substituting this into the previous inequality yields

ℒ⁡(C¯)≤ℒ⁡(C).\mathcal{L}(\overline{C})\ \leq\ \mathcal{L}(C).

∎

Corollary E.3.

An optimal solution of minC⁡ℒ⁡(C)\min_{C}\mathcal{L}(C) can be chosen among classwise permutation equivariant matrices.

We next characterize the algebraic structure of all classwise permutation equivariant matrices, which will serve as the reduced parameter space in which the optimization can be carried out according to Corollary E.3.

Lemma E.4.

Let 𝒢=∏a=1k𝔖na\mathcal{G}=\prod_{a=1}^{k}\mathfrak{S}_{n_{a}} act on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} by permuting the coordinates within each class VaV_{a}. A matrix C∈ℝn×nC\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is classwise permutation equivariant if and only if there exist real scalars {αa,βa}a=1k\{\alpha_{a},\beta_{a}\}_{a=1}^{k} and {γa​b}a≠b\{\gamma_{ab}\}_{a\neq b} such that

C=∑a=1k(αa​IVa+βa​JVa)+∑a≠bγa​b​JVa,Vb,C=\sum_{a=1}^{k}\big(\alpha_{a}I_{V_{a}}+\beta_{a}J_{V_{a}}\big)+\sum_{a\neq b}\gamma_{ab}\,J_{V_{a},V_{b}}, (10)

where:

  • •

    IVaI_{V_{a}} denotes the identity matrix on the coordinates indexed by VaV_{a};

  • •

    JVaJ_{V_{a}} is the na×nan_{a}\times n_{a} all-ones matrix;

  • •

    JVa,VbJ_{V_{a},V_{b}} is the na×nbn_{a}\times n_{b} all-ones block between classes aa and bb.

Equivalently, the commutant of the representation of 𝒢\mathcal{G} on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is spanned by the matrices {IVa,JVa,JVa,Vb:a≠b}\{I_{V_{a}},J_{V_{a}},J_{V_{a},V_{b}}:a\neq b\}.

Proof.

Let CC commute with every Pπ∈𝒢P_{\pi}\in\mathcal{G}. Since 𝒢\mathcal{G} acts independently on each class block, the condition Pπ​C=C​PπP_{\pi}C=CP_{\pi} decomposes into intra-class and inter-class parts.

Intra-class blocks:

Fix a class aa and consider CVa,VaC_{V_{a},V_{a}}, the submatrix of CC with both rows and columns indexed by the nodes in VaV_{a}. For any πa∈𝔖na\pi_{a}\in\mathfrak{S}_{n_{a}}, Pπa​CVa,Va=CVa,Va​PπaP_{\pi_{a}}C_{V_{a},V_{a}}=C_{V_{a},V_{a}}P_{\pi_{a}}. It is a classical result that the commutant of the full symmetric group acting by permutation matrices on ℝna\mathbb{R}^{n_{a}} is two-dimensional, spanned by IVaI_{V_{a}} and JVaJ_{V_{a}}. Hence there exist scalars αa,βa\alpha_{a},\beta_{a} such that CVa,Va=αa​IVa+βa​JVaC_{V_{a},V_{a}}=\alpha_{a}I_{V_{a}}+\beta_{a}J_{V_{a}}.

Inter-class blocks:

For a≠ba\neq b, consider CVa,VbC_{V_{a},V_{b}}. The commutation condition with independent permutations PπaP_{\pi_{a}} on VaV_{a} and PπbP_{\pi_{b}} on VbV_{b} implies

Pπa​CVa,Vb​Pπb⊤=CVa,Vb,∀(πa,πb)∈𝔖na×𝔖nb.P_{\pi_{a}}\,C_{V_{a},V_{b}}\,P_{\pi_{b}}^{\top}=C_{V_{a},V_{b}},\qquad\forall\,(\pi_{a},\pi_{b})\in\mathfrak{S}_{n_{a}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{n_{b}}.

The only matrices invariant under left and right actions of the full symmetric groups are constant matrices, i.e. scalar multiples of the all-ones block JVa,VbJ_{V_{a},V_{b}}. Thus there exists γa​b∈ℝ\gamma_{ab}\in\mathbb{R} such that CVa,Vb=γa​b​JVa,VbC_{V_{a},V_{b}}=\gamma_{ab}J_{V_{a},V_{b}}. Combining all blocks yields (10).

Conversely, any CC of the form (10) clearly commutes with every Pπ∈𝒢P_{\pi}\in\mathcal{G}, so the characterization is complete. ∎

Corollary E.5.

For any matrix C∈ℝn×nC\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, its Reynolds average C¯=𝔼π∼Unif⁡(𝒢)​[Pπ​C​Pπ⊤]\overline{C}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{G})}[P_{\pi}CP_{\pi}^{\top}] lies in the commutant characterized in Lemma E.4 and thus admits the representation (10).

We then turn to the statistical objective ℒ⁡(C)\mathcal{L}(C) and express it in a form amenable to optimization.

Lemma E.6.

Let Y=C​XY=CX and write Dτ:=⨁a=1kτa​IVaD_{\tau}:=\bigoplus_{a=1}^{k}\tau_{a}I_{V_{a}}. For any CC and any p∈Vap\in V_{a},

𝔼​Yp=∑b=1kCp,Vb​(𝟏nb​mb⊤),tr​Var​(Yp)=∑b=1kτb​‖Cp,Vb‖22.\mathbb{E}\,Y_{p}\ =\ \sum_{b=1}^{k}C_{p,V_{b}}\,(\mathbf{1}_{n_{b}}m_{b}^{\top}),\qquad\mathrm{tr\,Var}(Y_{p})\ =\ \sum_{b=1}^{k}\tau_{b}\,\|C_{p,V_{b}}\|_{2}^{2}.

Consequently,

ℒ⁡(C)=∑a=1k1na​∑p∈Va‖𝔼​Yp−ma‖22⏟squared bias+∑a=1k1na​∑p∈Va∑b=1kτb​‖Cp,Vb‖22⏟variance.\mathcal{L}(C)\ =\ \underbrace{\sum_{a=1}^{k}\frac{1}{n_{a}}\sum_{p\in V_{a}}\big\|\mathbb{E}Y_{p}-m_{a}\big\|_{2}^{2}}_{\text{\emph{squared bias}}}\ +\ \underbrace{\sum_{a=1}^{k}\frac{1}{n_{a}}\sum_{p\in V_{a}}\sum_{b=1}^{k}\tau_{b}\,\|C_{p,V_{b}}\|_{2}^{2}}_{\text{\emph{variance}}}. (11)
Proof.

For each class bb, the random vectors {xj:j∈Vb}\{x_{j}:j\in V_{b}\} are i.i.d. with 𝔼⁡[xj]=mb\mathbb{E}[x_{j}]=m_{b} and Cov⁡(xj)=Σb\operatorname{Cov}(x_{j})=\Sigma_{b}. Hence

𝔼⁡[XVb]=𝟏nb​mb⊤.\mathbb{E}[X_{V_{b}}]=\mathbf{1}_{n_{b}}m_{b}^{\top}.

Let Cp,Vb∈ℝ1×nbC_{p,V_{b}}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times n_{b}} denote the row of CC restricted to columns VbV_{b}. By classwise independence,

Var⁡(Cp,Vb​XVb)=∑j∈VbCp​j2​Σb=‖Cp,Vb‖22​Σb,\operatorname{Var}\!\big(C_{p,V_{b}}X_{V_{b}}\big)=\sum_{j\in V_{b}}C_{pj}^{2}\,\Sigma_{b}=\|C_{p,V_{b}}\|_{2}^{2}\,\Sigma_{b},

so that

𝔼​‖Cp,Vb​(XVb−𝔼​XVb)‖22=tr⁡[Var⁡(Cp,Vb​XVb)]=‖Cp,Vb‖22​tr⁡(Σb)=τb​‖Cp,Vb‖22.\mathbb{E}\big\|C_{p,V_{b}}(X_{V_{b}}-\mathbb{E}X_{V_{b}})\big\|_{2}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}\!\big[\operatorname{Var}(C_{p,V_{b}}X_{V_{b}})\big]=\|C_{p,V_{b}}\|_{2}^{2}\,\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{b})=\tau_{b}\|C_{p,V_{b}}\|_{2}^{2}.

Finally, using the bias–variance identity

𝔼​‖Z−m‖22=‖𝔼​Z−m‖22+tr⁡Var⁡(Z),\mathbb{E}\|Z-m\|_{2}^{2}=\|\mathbb{E}Z-m\|_{2}^{2}+\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}(Z),

and substituting Z=Yp=Cp,;​XZ=Y_{p}=C_{p,;}X, we obtain (11). ∎

Corollary E.7.

Suppose CC is classwise permutation equivariant, i.e. it has the form (10). Then, for any p∈Vap\in V_{a},

𝔼​Yp=(αa+βa​na)​ma+∑b≠aγa​b​nb​mb,\mathbb{E}Y_{p}\ =\ (\alpha_{a}+\beta_{a}n_{a})\,m_{a}\ +\ \sum_{b\neq a}\gamma_{ab}n_{b}\,m_{b},

and, writing τb:=tr⁡(Σb)\tau_{b}:=\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_{b}),

tr​Var​(Yp)=τa​((αa+βa)2+(na−1)​βa2)+∑b≠aτb​nb​γa​b2.\mathrm{tr\,Var}(Y_{p})\ =\ \tau_{a}\Big((\alpha_{a}+\beta_{a})^{2}+(n_{a}-1)\beta_{a}^{2}\Big)\ +\ \sum_{b\neq a}\tau_{b}n_{b}\gamma_{ab}^{2}.

Consequently, the per-class contribution to the loss equals the quadratic

ϕa(αa,βa,γa∙)=∥ua+M−aγa∙∥22+τa((αa+βa)2+(na−1)βa2)+γa∙⊤D−aγa∙,\phi_{a}(\alpha_{a},\beta_{a},\gamma_{a\bullet})=\Big\|\,u_{a}+M_{-a}\gamma_{a\bullet}\,\Big\|_{2}^{2}+\tau_{a}\Big((\alpha_{a}+\beta_{a})^{2}+(n_{a}-1)\beta_{a}^{2}\Big)+\gamma_{a\bullet}^{\top}D_{-a}\gamma_{a\bullet}, (12)

where γa∙≔(γa​b)b≠a∈ℝk−1\gamma_{a\bullet}\coloneqq(\gamma_{ab})_{b\neq a}\in\mathbb{R}^{k-1}, ua≔(αa+na​βa−1)​mau_{a}\coloneqq(\alpha_{a}+n_{a}\beta_{a}-1)m_{a}, M−a=[nb​mb]b≠a∈ℝd×(k−1)M_{-a}=[\,n_{b}m_{b}\,]_{b\neq a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times(k-1)}, D−a=diag​(τb​nb)b≠a⪰0D_{-a}=\mathrm{diag}(\tau_{b}n_{b})_{b\neq a}\succeq 0.

Theorem E.8.

Under the model assumed in Section E.1.1, the minimizer of minC⁡ℒ⁡(C)\min_{C}\mathcal{L}(C) has the following block structure.

(1) Intra-class blocks. For each class aa,

(C⋆)a​a=αa⋆​IVa+βa⋆​JVa.(C^{\star})_{aa}=\alpha_{a}^{\star}I_{V_{a}}+\beta_{a}^{\star}J_{V_{a}}.
  • •

    If na>1n_{a}>1, then αa⋆=0\alpha_{a}^{\star}=0 and

    βa⋆=Aana​Aa+τa,Aa=‖ma‖22−∑b≠ac≠anb​nc​⟨ma,mb⟩​[(G−a+D−a)−1]b​c​⟨mc,ma⟩,\beta_{a}^{\star}=\frac{A_{a}}{\,n_{a}A_{a}+\tau_{a}\,},\ A_{a}=\|m_{a}\|_{2}^{2}-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\neq a\\ c\neq a\end{subarray}}n_{b}n_{c}\,\langle m_{a},m_{b}\rangle\big[(G_{-a}+D_{-a})^{-1}\big]_{bc}\langle m_{c},m_{a}\rangle,

    where G−aG_{-a} and D−aD_{-a} are defined in Corollary E.7.

  • •

    If na=1n_{a}=1, the objective depends only on αa+βa\alpha_{a}+\beta_{a}, and one may set αa⋆=0\alpha_{a}^{\star}=0 without loss of generality.

(C⋆)a​b=γa​b⋆​JVa,Vb,(C^{\star})_{ab}=\gamma_{ab}^{\star}\,J_{V_{a},V_{b}},

where the coefficients γa​b⋆\gamma_{ab}^{\star} satisfy the linear system

∑c≠a(G−a+D−a)b​c​γa​c⋆=(1−na​βa⋆)​nb​⟨ma,mb⟩,b≠a.\sum_{c\neq a}(G_{-a}+D_{-a})_{bc}\,\gamma_{ac}^{\star}=(1-n_{a}\beta_{a}^{\star})\,n_{b}\,\langle m_{a},m_{b}\rangle,\quad b\neq a.

Equivalently, solving for γa​b⋆\gamma_{ab}^{\star} gives

γa​b⋆=τana​Aa+τa​∑c≠a[(G−a+D−a)−1]b​c​nc​⟨ma,mc⟩.\gamma_{ab}^{\star}=\frac{\tau_{a}}{\,n_{a}A_{a}+\tau_{a}\,}\sum_{c\neq a}\big[(G_{-a}+D_{-a})^{-1}\big]_{bc}\,n_{c}\,\langle m_{a},m_{c}\rangle.

The minimizer C⋆C^{\star} is unique.

Proof.

By Corollary E.3, we may restrict to the commutant form (10). Fix a class aa. From Corollary E.7, the per-class contribution of VaV_{a} to ℒ⁡(C)\mathcal{L}(C) is (12).

Convexity and strict convexity:

For each class aa, recall from (12) that

ϕa(αa,βa,γa∙)=∥ua+M−aγa∙∥22+τa((αa+βa)2+(na−1)βa2)+γa∙⊤D−aγa∙,\phi_{a}(\alpha_{a},\beta_{a},\gamma_{a\bullet})=\Big\|\,u_{a}+M_{-a}\gamma_{a\bullet}\,\Big\|_{2}^{2}+\tau_{a}\Big((\alpha_{a}+\beta_{a})^{2}+(n_{a}-1)\beta_{a}^{2}\Big)+\gamma_{a\bullet}^{\top}D_{-a}\gamma_{a\bullet},

where ua=(αa+na​βa−1)​mau_{a}=(\alpha_{a}+n_{a}\beta_{a}-1)m_{a}, M−a=[nb​mb]b≠aM_{-a}=[\,n_{b}m_{b}\,]_{b\neq a}, and D−a=diag​(τb​nb)b≠a≻0D_{-a}=\mathrm{diag}(\tau_{b}n_{b})_{b\neq a}\succ 0 as we assume any τb>0\tau_{b}>0 in Section E.1.1. The Hessian of ϕa\phi_{a} with respect to (αa,βa,γa∙)(\alpha_{a},\beta_{a},\gamma_{a\bullet}) is the block matrix

Ha=2​[ABB⊤G−a+D−a],A=[‖ma‖22+τana​‖ma‖22+τana​‖ma‖22+τana2​‖ma‖22+na​τa],B=[ha⊤na​ha⊤],H_{a}=2\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\ B^{\top}&G_{-a}+D_{-a}\end{bmatrix},\qquad A=\begin{bmatrix}\|m_{a}\|_{2}^{2}+\tau_{a}&n_{a}\|m_{a}\|_{2}^{2}+\tau_{a}\\[2.0pt] n_{a}\|m_{a}\|_{2}^{2}+\tau_{a}&n_{a}^{2}\|m_{a}\|_{2}^{2}+n_{a}\tau_{a}\end{bmatrix},\quad B=\begin{bmatrix}h_{a}^{\top}\\[2.0pt] n_{a}\,h_{a}^{\top}\end{bmatrix},

Each term in (12) is a nonnegative quadratic form: the first term is a squared Euclidean norm, the second is τa\tau_{a} times a positive semidefinite quadratic in (αa,βa)(\alpha_{a},\beta_{a}), and the last is γa∙⊤D−aγa∙\gamma_{a\bullet}^{\top}D_{-a}\gamma_{a\bullet} with D−a≻0D_{-a}\succ 0. Ha≻0⟺A≻0andS:=G−a+D−a−B⊤A−1B≻0.H_{a}\succ 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A\succ 0\ \text{and}\ S:=G_{-a}+D_{-a}-B^{\top}A^{-1}B\succ 0.

A direct calculation gives

detA=τa​(na−1)​(na​‖ma‖22+τa),A11=‖ma‖22+τa>0.\det A=\tau_{a}\,(n_{a}-1)\,(n_{a}\|m_{a}\|_{2}^{2}+\tau_{a}),\qquad A_{11}=\|m_{a}\|_{2}^{2}+\tau_{a}>0.

Hence A≻0A\succ 0 if and only if na>1n_{a}>1 and τa>0\tau_{a}>0. Under these assumptions, we compute

B⊤​A−1​B=c​ha​ha⊤,c=nana​‖ma‖22+τa∈(0,1‖ma‖22),B^{\top}A^{-1}B=c\,h_{a}h_{a}^{\top},\qquad c=\frac{n_{a}}{\,n_{a}\|m_{a}\|_{2}^{2}+\tau_{a}\,}\in\Bigl(0,\frac{1}{\|m_{a}\|_{2}^{2}}\Bigr),

S=(G−a−c​ha​ha⊤)+D−a.S=(G_{-a}-c\,h_{a}h_{a}^{\top})+D_{-a}.

For any v∈ℝk−1v\in\mathbb{R}^{k-1}, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality yields

v⊤​(G−a−c​ha​ha⊤)​v=‖M−a​v‖22−c​⟨ma,M−a​v⟩2≥(1−c​‖ma‖22)​‖M−a​v‖22.v^{\top}(G_{-a}-c\,h_{a}h_{a}^{\top})v=\|M_{-a}v\|_{2}^{2}-c\,\langle m_{a},M_{-a}v\rangle^{2}\ \geq\ (1-c\|m_{a}\|_{2}^{2})\,\|M_{-a}v\|_{2}^{2}.

Eliminating γa∙\gamma_{a\bullet}:

For fixed (αa,βa)(\alpha_{a},\beta_{a}),

∇γϕa=2M−a⊤(ua+M−aγa∙)+2D−aγa∙.\nabla_{\gamma}\phi_{a}=2M_{-a}^{\top}(u_{a}+M_{-a}\gamma_{a\bullet})+2D_{-a}\gamma_{a\bullet}.

Setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equations

(G−a+D−a)γa∙+M−a⊤ua=0.(G_{-a}+D_{-a})\,\gamma_{a\bullet}+M_{-a}^{\top}u_{a}=0.

γa∙⋆(αa,βa)=−(G−a+D−a)−1M−a⊤ua=−(αa+naβa−1)(G−a+D−a)−1ha.\gamma_{a\bullet}^{\star}(\alpha_{a},\beta_{a})=-(G_{-a}+D_{-a})^{-1}M_{-a}^{\top}u_{a}=-(\alpha_{a}+n_{a}\beta_{a}-1)\,(G_{-a}+D_{-a})^{-1}h_{a}. (13)
Solving for αa⋆\alpha_{a}^{\star}, βa⋆\beta_{a}^{\star} and γa∙⋆\gamma_{a\bullet}^{\star}:

Define the reduced function

ϕ~a(αa,βa):=minγϕa(αa,βa,γ)=ϕa(αa,βa,γa∙⋆(αa,βa)).\tilde{\phi}_{a}(\alpha_{a},\beta_{a}):=\min_{\gamma}\phi_{a}(\alpha_{a},\beta_{a},\gamma)=\phi_{a}(\alpha_{a},\beta_{a},\gamma_{a\bullet}^{\star}(\alpha_{a},\beta_{a})).

Because ϕa\phi_{a} is convex-quadratic and the minimizer in γ\gamma is unique, the envelope theorem implies that the partial derivatives of ϕ~a\tilde{\phi}_{a} are simply the partial derivatives of ϕa\phi_{a} evaluated at γa∙⋆\gamma_{a\bullet}^{\star}; that is,

∂ϕ~a∂αa=∂ϕa∂αa|γ=γa∙⋆,∂ϕ~a∂βa=∂ϕa∂βa|γ=γa∙⋆.\frac{\partial\tilde{\phi}_{a}}{\partial\alpha_{a}}=\left.\frac{\partial\phi_{a}}{\partial\alpha_{a}}\right|_{\gamma=\gamma_{a\bullet}^{\star}},\qquad\frac{\partial\tilde{\phi}_{a}}{\partial\beta_{a}}=\left.\frac{\partial\phi_{a}}{\partial\beta_{a}}\right|_{\gamma=\gamma_{a\bullet}^{\star}}.

When features are sampled from a high-dimensional distribution, the optimal convolution is nearly block-diagonal, and its intra-class coefficients asymptotically approach a deterministic limit. We restate and prove Theorem 4.1 as follows.

E.2 Spectral GNNs Cannot Express the Optimal Convolution

Definition E.10.

Let L∈ℝn×nL\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be a real symmetric matrix, e.g. a graph Laplacian. Denote by

spec(L)={λ1<λ2<⋯<λm}\mathrm{spec}(L)=\{\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}<\cdots<\lambda_{m}\}

the set of distinct eigenvalues of LL, and let each λ\lambda have multiplicity mλ=dimker⁡(L−λ​I)m_{\lambda}=\dim\ker(L-\lambda I). For each λ∈spec⁡(L)\lambda\in\mathrm{spec}(L), let Uλ∈ℝn×mλU_{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m_{\lambda}} collect an orthonormal basis of ker⁡(L−λ​I)\ker(L-\lambda I). Define the orthogonal projector onto this eigenspace by

Eλ:=Uλ​Uλ⊤.E_{\lambda}\;:=\;U_{\lambda}U_{\lambda}^{\top}.
Remark E.11.

Then {Eλ}λ∈spec⁡(L)\{E_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda\in\mathrm{spec}(L)} satisfies

Eλ⊤=Eλ,Eλ2=Eλ,Eλ​Eμ=0​(λ≠μ),∑λ∈spec⁡(L)Eλ=In,E_{\lambda}^{\top}=E_{\lambda},\quad E_{\lambda}^{2}=E_{\lambda},\quad E_{\lambda}E_{\mu}=0\ (\lambda\neq\mu),\quad\sum_{\lambda\in\mathrm{spec}(L)}E_{\lambda}=I_{n},

and the spectral resolution

L=∑λ∈spec⁡(L)λ​Eλ.L\;=\;\sum_{\lambda\in\mathrm{spec}(L)}\lambda\,E_{\lambda}.

Moreover, EλE_{\lambda} is independent of the choice of orthonormal basis UλU_{\lambda}.

To simplify the discussion, we assume the feature dimension d→+∞d\to+\infty, under which the optimal convolution minimizing ℒ⁡(C)\mathcal{L}(C) becomes block-diagonal:

(C⋆)a​a=1na+τa,(C⋆)a​b=0​(b≠a).(C^{\star})_{aa}=\frac{1}{n_{a}+\tau_{a}},\qquad(C^{\star})_{ab}=0\ (b\neq a).

From the viewpoint of expressiveness, our discussion concerns not a single operator but an entire family of convolution operators parameterized by learnable coefficients. A spectral GNN corresponds to the family

𝒮=span⁡{Eλ:λ∈spec⁡(L)}={C⁡(g)=∑λg⁡(λ)​Eλ:g∈ℝspec⁡(L)},\mathcal{S}=\mathrm{span}\{E_{\lambda}:\lambda\in\mathrm{spec}(L)\}=\{\,C(g)=\textstyle\sum_{\lambda}g(\lambda)\,E_{\lambda}:\ g\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathrm{spec}(L)}\,\},

that is, all linear filters expressible as functions of the Laplacian LL. The expressive power of this model family depends on whether, through learning, it can realize or approximate the desired target convolution C⋆C^{\star}.

We show that the optimal convolution C⋆C^{\star} lies strictly outside this spectral subspace and cannot even be approximated within it to arbitrary accuracy. In other words, no choice of spectral coefficients g⁡(λ)g(\lambda) can reproduce or arbitrarily approach C⋆C^{\star}. In analogy with control theory, the family of spectral convolutions is structurally unreachable from C⋆C^{\star}, indicating that this function class is inherently incapable of reaching the optimal convolution during learning, and thereby revealing a fundamental limitation in its representational capacity. We restate and prove Theorem 4.2 as follows.

Theorem E.12.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a connected graph with Laplacian eigendecomposition L=∑λ∈spec⁡(L)λ​EλL=\sum_{\lambda\in\mathrm{spec}(L)}\lambda\,E_{\lambda} as in the definition above, and |V|=n|V|=n. Define the class of spectral convolution matrices

𝒞:={C⁡(c)=∑λ∈spec⁡(L)cλ​Eλ:c=(cλ)λ∈spec⁡(L)∈ℝm},\mathcal{C}\;:=\;\Bigl\{\,C(c)\;=\;\sum_{\lambda\in\mathrm{spec}(L)}c_{\lambda}\,E_{\lambda}\ :\ c=(c_{\lambda})_{\lambda\in\mathrm{spec}(L)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\,\Bigr\},

where m=|spec⁡(L)|m=|\mathrm{spec}(L)|. Each C⁡(c)C(c) applies a scalar response cλc_{\lambda} to the entire eigenspace of eigenvalue λ\lambda.

Then there exists an integer K≥1K\geq 1 such that, for any integer K<k≤nK<k\leq n, there exists a kk-partition V=V1∪⋯∪VkV=V_{1}\cup\cdots\cup V_{k}, with labels yi=ty_{i}=t if and only if vi∈Vtv_{i}\in V_{t}, having the following property: if C⁡(c)∈𝒞C(c)\in\mathcal{C} satisfies

C​(c)i​j=0whenever ​yi≠yj,C(c)_{ij}=0\quad\text{whenever }y_{i}\neq y_{j},

then necessarily C⁡(c)=α​InC(c)=\alpha I_{n} for some α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}.

To prove the theorem, we begin with some preparations.

Definition E.13 (Indexing conventions).

Let M∈ℝa×bM\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times b} be a matrix.

  • •

    For a row index i∈[a]i\in[a], we denote by M−i∈ℝ(a−1)×bM_{-i}\in\mathbb{R}^{(a-1)\times b} the matrix obtained by removing the ii-th row of MM.

    For row and column indices i∈[a]i\in[a] and j∈[b]j\in[b], we denote by M−i,−j∈ℝ(a−1)×(b−1)M_{-i,-j}\in\mathbb{R}^{(a-1)\times(b-1)} the matrix obtained by removing the ii-th row and the jj-th column of MM.

Di:=diag⁡(u1​(i),u2​(i),…,un​(i))∈ℝn×n.D_{i}\;:=\;\operatorname{diag}\big(u_{1}(i),u_{2}(i),\dots,u_{n}(i)\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.

Define

Mi:=U−i​Di∈ℝ(n−1)×n.M_{i}\;:=\;U_{-i}\,D_{i}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{(n-1)\times n}.

We will collect a vertical stack of such matrices so that each newly added block activates at least one previously-zero column and together they cover all columns:

Definition E.14.

Let I=(i1,…,ir)I=(i_{1},\dots,i_{r}) be an ordered list of vertices, and define the stacked matrix

MI:=[Mi1Mir]∈ℝr⁡(n−1)×n.M_{I}\;:=\;\begin{bmatrix}M_{i_{1}}\\[2.0pt] \vdots\\[2.0pt] M_{i_{r}}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{r(n-1)\times n}.

For each vertex i∈Vi\in V, denote by

Si:={ℓ∈[n]:(Mi):,ℓ≠0}S_{i}\;:=\;\{\ell\in[n]:(M_{i})_{:,\ell}\neq 0\}

the set of column indices activated by MiM_{i}.

We say that II is column-activating if it satisfies

  • •

    Every column of MIM_{I} contains at least one nonzero entry, i.e. ⋃k=1rSik=[n].\bigcup_{k=1}^{r}S_{i_{k}}=[n].

  • •

    Each step kk introduces a new activation, i.e. ∃ℓ∈Sik∖⋃t<kSit.\exists\,\ell\in S_{i_{k}}\setminus\bigcup_{t<k}S_{i_{t}}. Equivalently, MikM_{i_{k}} contributes a nonzero entry in a column that was entirely zero in the previous partial stack [Mi1;…;Mik−1][M_{i_{1}};\dots;M_{i_{k-1}}].

We call such an index list II minimal if it is inclusion-minimal with respect to the activated columns, namely

⋃i∈JSi=⋃i∈ISi⟹J=Ifor all ​J⊆I.\bigcup_{i\in J}S_{i}=\bigcup_{i\in I}S_{i}\;\Longrightarrow\;J=I\quad\text{for all }J\subseteq I.
Remark E.15 (Greedy construction).

The greedy rule produces a column-activating list II. Starting from the empty cover S(0):=∅S^{(0)}:=\varnothing, we iteratively choose nodes that maximally enlarge the current coverage:

ik:=arg⁡maxi∈V​|Si∖S(k−1)|,S(k):=S(k−1)∪Sik.i_{k}\;:=\;\arg\max_{i\in V}\;\bigl|\,S_{i}\setminus S^{(k-1)}\,\bigr|,\qquad S^{(k)}\;:=\;S^{(k-1)}\cup S_{i_{k}}.

The process stops once S(k)=[n]S^{(k)}=[n], meaning each column of MIM_{I} is nonzero in some block MitM_{i_{t}}. The resulting index list I=(i1,i2,…,iK)I=(i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{K}) is column-activating.

While we do not rely on the optimality of its length, each selected block MikM_{i_{k}} strictly increases the coverage S(k)S^{(k)}, so the greedy rule yields a minimal column-activating list in the sense of Definition E.14.

Proposition E.16.

Let U=[u1,…,un]∈ℝn×nU=[u_{1},\dots,u_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be an orthogonal matrix U⊤​U=InU^{\top}U=I_{n}, and let Uk=[u1,…,uk]∈ℝn×kU_{k}=[u_{1},\dots,u_{k}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k} with 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n. Fix an index s∈{1,…,n}s\in\{1,\dots,n\}, and let es∈ℝne_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denote the ss-th standard basis vector. Define the row-selection matrix

Single block analysis:

Multi–block induction:

Let I=(i1,…,iK)I=(i_{1},\dots,i_{K}) be any minimal column–activating list and define S(r):=⋃t=1rSitS^{(r)}:=\bigcup_{t=1}^{r}S_{i_{t}}. By induction with the two–block formula above,

rank​[Mi1Mir]=|S(r)|−1(r=1,2,…,K),\mathrm{rank}\!\begin{bmatrix}M_{i_{1}}\\ \vdots\\ M_{i_{r}}\end{bmatrix}=|S^{(r)}|-1\quad(r=1,2,\dots,K),

The above reasoning does not rely on the spectrum being simple. Let

W=⨁λ∈spec⁡(L)span{𝟏mλ}={c=∑λαλ 1mλ}.W\;=\;\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\mathrm{spec}(L)}\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{1}_{m_{\lambda}}\}\;=\;\bigl\{\,c=\sum_{\lambda}\alpha_{\lambda}\,\mathbf{1}_{m_{\lambda}}\bigr\}.
