Remark E.19.

In practice, for many real-world graphs the minimal activating length KK is often K=1K=1, since there typically exists at least one vertex ii whose corresponding Laplacian eigenvector coordinates {uℓ​(i)}ℓ=1n\{u_{\ell}(i)\}_{\ell=1}^{n} are all nonzero. In such cases, the bipartition obtained by isolating this single vertex already achieves rank⁡(MI)=n−1\operatorname{rank}(M_{I})=n-1 and thus suffices to guarantee C⁡(c)=α​InC(c)=\alpha I_{n}.

Corollary E.20.

Assume that at least one class contains more than one node. Then the optimal convolution C⋆C^{\star} lies at a positive distance from the spectral convolution subspace 𝒮=span⁡{Eλ:λ∈spec⁡(L)}\mathcal{S}=\mathrm{span}\{E_{\lambda}:\lambda\in\mathrm{spec}(L)\}.

Proof.

Under this assumption, C⋆C^{\star} has the block-diagonal form

(C⋆)a​a=1na+τa,(C⋆)a​b=0​(b≠a),(C^{\star})_{aa}=\frac{1}{n_{a}+\tau_{a}},\qquad(C^{\star})_{ab}=0\ (b\neq a),

and hence all inter-class blocks vanish. Since at least one block has size greater than one, C⋆C^{\star} is not a scalar multiple of the identity. By Theorem E.12, any spectral convolution matrix C⁡(g)=∑λg⁡(λ)​EλC(g)=\sum_{\lambda}g(\lambda)E_{\lambda} with vanishing inter-class entries must collapse to a scalar multiple of the identity. Therefore no choice of coefficients g⁡(λ)g(\lambda) can yield C⁡(g)=C⋆C(g)=C^{\star}, i.e. the system of equations C⁡(g)=C⋆C(g)=C^{\star} has no solution. As 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a finite-dimensional (hence closed) subspace of the matrix space ℝn×n\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, a point outside it must have a strictly positive distance to it. Consequently, dist⁡(C⋆,𝒮)>0\operatorname{dist}(C^{\star},\mathcal{S})>0. ∎

Remark E.21.

Corollary E.20 implies that the spectral convolution family cannot represent the optimal convolution C⋆C^{\star}, nor can it approximate it arbitrarily closely. In fact, this limitation is robust: even if one perturbs C⋆C^{\star} slightly within the class of block-diagonal matrices with vanishing inter-class entries, no spectral convolution can realize or approximate these perturbed operators either. The reason is structural rather than numerical: according to Theorem E.12, as long as at least one class contains more than one node and the inter-class interference is suppressed (Ca​b=0C_{ab}=0 for a≠ba\neq b), any nontrivial intra-class variation leads to matrices that fall outside the spectral subspace. This shows that the expressive capacity of spectral convolutions is severely constrained by their diagonal structure in the spectral domain.

Appendix F Experimental Details

All experiments are run on a GPU NVIDIA RTX A6000 with 48G memory.

F.1 Heterophilic Node Classification

Datasets

The dataset statistics, including the numbers of nodes and edges, feature dimensionality, number of node classes, and edge homophily ratios, are summarized in Table 6.

Hyperparameter Setting

For all datasets, we train for at most 1,0001{,}000 epochs with early stopping (patience =200=200). On the four large heterophilic datasets (Roman Empire, Tolokers, Minesweeper, Questions), we fix the MLP hidden size to 512512 and the polynomial order to 55. For the remaining datasets, we use a hidden size of 6464 and set the polynomial order to 22.

We perform a grid search over the training hyperparameters of FSpecGNN, including the dropout rate, learning rate, weight decay, and the number of GAT heads. The corresponding search ranges are reported in Table 7.

F.2 GNN Expressivity

For all tasks, we use the distance-encoding hyperparameter max_dis=5=5. Since spectral models can achieve long-range propagation with fewer layers than spatial models, we use depth L=2L=2 with hidden dimension d=150d=150 for most tasks. For edge-level homomorphism-counting tasks, we use L=3L=3 and d=128d=128 to match the parameter budget. The parameter counts are reported in the table 8.

Time and Space Overhead

We report the average iteration time and the peak GPU memory usage for each task in Table 10. We also provide a visual mapping between task names and their corresponding substructures in Table 9.
